formalMeaning.en: A multi-chevron hazard marker board indicating a sharp change of direction to the right, mounted facing approaching traffic on the outside of the curve.

testHint.af: Verskeie rooi chevrons op 'n ry wat almal een kant toe wys beteken 'n skerp draai daardie kant toe — hier links.
testHint.en: Several red chevrons in a row all pointing one way mean a sharp bend that way – left here.

behaviour.af: Verminder spoed lank voor die draai en volg die pad na links in die rigting waarheen die chevrons wys.
behaviour.en: Reduce speed well before the curve and follow the road to the left in the direction the chevrons point.

plainEnglish.af: 'n Skerp draai na links is voor. Die herhaalde chevrons beklemtoon hoe skerp die draai is.
plainEnglish.en: A sharp curve to the left is ahead. The repeated chevrons stress how sharp the bend is.

commonMistake.af: Om die veelvuldige chevrons as verskeie afsonderlike draaie te lees; hulle beskryf almal een skerp draai in dieselfde rigting.
commonMistake.en: Reading the multiple chevrons as several separate turns; they all describe one sharp bend in the same direction.

formalMeaning.af: 'n Multi-chevron-gevaarbakenbord wat 'n skerp rigtingverandering na links aandui, gemonteer na aankomende verkeer aan die buitekant van die draai.
formalMeaning.en: A multi-chevron hazard marker board indicating a sharp change of direction to the left, mounted facing approaching traffic on the outside of the curve.

testHint.af: Chevrons wat van die middel af albei kante toe wys beteken die pad verdeel links en regs — 'n T-aansluiting voor.
testHint.en: Chevrons pointing both ways from the middle mean the road splits left and right – a T-junction ahead.

behaviour.af: Ry stadiger met nadering, gee voorrang soos vereis, en draai links of regs — jy kan nie reguit aanhou nie.
behaviour.en: Slow down on approach, give way as required, and turn left or right – you cannot continue straight ahead.

plainEnglish.af: Die pad waarop jy is eindig by 'n T-aansluiting voor. Jy sal óf links óf regs moet draai.
plainEnglish.en: The road you are on ends at a T-junction ahead. You will have to turn either left or right.

commonMistake.af: Om te aanvaar jy mag reguit aanhou; die uitwaartse chevrons beteken die pad eindig hier en jy moet draai.
commonMistake.en: Assuming you may carry on straight; the diverging chevrons mean the road ends here and you must turn.

formalMeaning.af: 'n Gevaarbakenbord, met chevrons wat na buite in albei rigtings wys, gemonteer na verkeer wat die stam van 'n T-aansluiting nader waar die deurpad eindig.
formalMeaning.en: A hazard marker board, with chevrons pointing outward in both directions, mounted facing traffic approaching the stem of a T-junction where the through road terminates.

signs.name: Dead end or road closed chevron

testHint.af: Chevrons wat na binne na die middel toe wys beteken die pad is toe — doodloop voor.
testHint.en: Chevrons pointing inward toward the middle mean the road is shut – dead end ahead.

behaviour.af: Stop of ry stadiger en draai om; moenie probeer om by die baken verby te gaan nie.
behaviour.en: Stop or slow down and turn around; do not attempt to pass the marker.

plainEnglish.af: Die pad voor is gesluit of loop dood. Jy kan nie deurry nie.
plainEnglish.en: The road ahead is closed or comes to a dead end. You cannot drive through.

commonMistake.af: Om dit met die T-aansluiting-bord te verwar; hier wys die chevrons na binne na mekaar toe, wat beteken die pad is versper, nie dat dit verdeel nie.
commonMistake.en: Confusing it with the T-junction board; here the chevrons point inward toward each other, meaning the way is blocked, not that it splits.

formalMeaning.af: 'n Gevaarbakenbord, met chevrons wat van albei kante af na binne saamloop, gemonteer na verkeer om die einde van 'n pad of 'n padsluiting voor te merk.
formalMeaning.en: A hazard marker board, with chevrons converging inward from both sides, mounted facing traffic to mark the end of a road or a road closure ahead.

testHint.af: 'n Rooi-en-wit gestreepte balk oor die pad is 'n boom — stop en wag dat dit oopmaak.
testHint.en: A red-and-white striped bar across the road is a boom – stop and wait for it to open.

behaviour.af: Stop voor die versperring en gaan eers verder sodra dit oopgemaak is of jy deurgewys word.
behaviour.en: Stop before the barrier and only proceed once it is opened or you are directed through.

plainEnglish.af: 'n Boom of versperring is oor die pad geplaas. Die hoësigbaarheid rooi-en-wit patroon merk die hindernis.
plainEnglish.en: A boom or barrier is placed across the road. The high-visibility red-and-white pattern marks the obstruction.

commonMistake.af: Om om die boom te probeer ry; die baken beteken die pad is fisies versper en mag nie verbygegaan word terwyl dit toe is nie.
commonMistake.en: Trying to drive around the boom; the marker means the road is physically blocked and must not be passed while closed.

formalMeaning.af: 'n Gevaarbaken wat aan 'n boom of versperring aangebring is wat die rypad fisies blokkeer of gedeeltelik blokkeer.
formalMeaning.en: A hazard marker fitted to a boom or barricade that physically blocks or partly blocks the roadway.

testHint.af: Die verdelingspatroonplaat merk waar die pad verdeel — kies jou kant vroeg en bly weg van die neus.
testHint.en: The split-pattern plate marks where the road divides – pick your side early and stay clear of the nose.

behaviour.af: Kies jou baan vroeg en hou aan jou kant van die baken; moenie ooit in die splitsingsneus inry of daaroor straal nie.
behaviour.en: Choose your lane early and keep to your side of the marker; never drive into or straddle the gore nose.

plainEnglish.af: Dit merk die neus van 'n punt waar die pad verdeel, soos waar 'n afrit die hoofpad verlaat. Hou aan een kant daarvan.
plainEnglish.en: This marks the nose of a point where the road splits, such as where an off-ramp leaves the main road. Keep to one side of it.

commonMistake.af: Om na die baken toe te dryf terwyl jy besluit watter kant toe om te gaan; die baankeuse moet gemaak word voordat jy die neus bereik.
commonMistake.en: Drifting toward the marker while deciding which way to go; the lane choice must be made before you reach the nose.

formalMeaning.af: 'n Splitsingsgebied-gevaarbaken wat by die fisiese verdeling (splitsing) tussen twee uiteenlopende rypaaie geplaas is, met die patroon wat verkeer wys om aan weerskante verby te gaan.
formalMeaning.en: A gore-area hazard marker placed at the physical division (gore) between two diverging roadways, with the pattern showing traffic to pass on either side.

testHint.af: Twee rooi pyle wat na mekaar wys = die punt waar bane verdeel. Kies 'n kant voordat jy dit bereik.
testHint.en: Two red arrows pointing at each other = the point where lanes split. Pick a side before you reach it.

behaviour.af: Bly in jou gekose baan en bly weg van die geverfde/geplaveide splitsingsgebied. Verbind jou vroeg om óf op die pad te bly óf die afrit te neem; moenie oor die baken straal of daaroor sny nie.
behaviour.en: Stay in your chosen lane and keep clear of the painted/paved gore area. Commit early to either staying on the road or taking the off-ramp; do not straddle or cut across the marker.

plainEnglish.af: Hierdie baken wys waar die pad verdeel, en merk die neus van die geplaveide driehoekige eiland (die splitsing) tussen 'n deurpad en 'n afrit of oprit. Dit waarsku jou om nie in of oor daardie wig pad te ry nie.
plainEnglish.en: This marker shows where the road splits, marking the nose of the paved triangular island (the gore) between a through-road and an exit or entrance ramp. It warns you not to drive into or across that wedge of road.

commonMistake.af: Om dit as 'n gewone rigtingteken te behandel en op die laaste oomblik oor die splitsing baan te probeer verwissel, of om oor die neus van die eiland te ry.
commonMistake.en: Treating it as a normal direction sign and trying to change lanes across the gore at the last moment, or driving over the nose of the island.

formalMeaning.af: 'n Splitsings-chevron-gevaarbaken wat die verdelende neus van die splitsingsgebied aandui waar twee rybane uiteenloop of saamvloei.
formalMeaning.en: A gore chevron hazard marker indicating the dividing nose of the gore area where two carriageways diverge or merge.

testHint.af: Rooi-en-wit strepe op iets oorhoofs = kyk op en kyk jou hoogte na voordat jy daaronder deurry.
testHint.en: Red-and-white stripes on something overhead = look up and check your height before you drive under it.

behaviour.af: Let op die waarskuwing en kyk of jou voertuig (insluitend enige vrag) veilig daaronder kan deurgaan. As die deurgangshoogte twyfelagtig is, ry stadiger en moenie onder die struktuur deurgaan nie.
behaviour.en: Note the warning and check that your vehicle (including any load) can safely pass underneath. If clearance is in doubt, slow down and do not proceed under the structure.

plainEnglish.af: 'n Rooi-en-wit gestreepte plaat wat aan 'n oorhoofse struktuur soos 'n lae brug, portaal of boom vasgemaak is om die hindernis te laat uitstaan en jou van beperkte deurgangshoogte voor te waarsku.
plainEnglish.en: A red-and-white striped plate fixed to an overhead structure such as a low bridge, gantry or boom to make the obstruction stand out and warn you of limited clearance ahead.

commonMistake.af: Om te aanvaar die strepe is bloot versiering en die hoogte-/deurgangsrisiko vir 'n hoë voertuig of vrag te ignoreer.
commonMistake.en: Assuming the stripes are purely decorative and ignoring the height/clearance risk for a tall vehicle or load.

formalMeaning.af: 'n Oorhoofse gevaarplaat-gevaarbaken wat 'n oorhoofse hindernis of beperkte vertikale deurgangshoogte uitlig.
formalMeaning.en: An overhead danger plate hazard marker highlighting an overhead obstruction or restricted vertical clearance.

questions.prompt: Which pedal do you press to slow the vehicle down?
options: Accelerator
Clutch
Brake
questions.explanation: The brake pedal slows and stops the vehicle. The accelerator increases engine speed and the clutch disconnects the engine from the wheels — neither slows you down.

questions.prompt: What is the clutch used for in a manual vehicle?
options: To make the vehicle go faster
To change gears smoothly by disconnecting the engine from the wheels
To sound the hooter
questions.explanation: Pressing the clutch temporarily disconnects the engine from the wheels so you can change gears without grinding them.

questions.prompt: Before driving off, the first thing you should do after getting in is:
options: Start the engine immediately
Adjust your seat and mirrors, and fasten your seatbelt
Select fifth gear
questions.explanation: Set up your seat and mirrors and belt up first so you have full control and visibility before the car moves.

questions.prompt: When should you use the handbrake?
options: Only when the vehicle breaks down
When parked, and to help hold the vehicle on a hill start
While driving at high speed
questions.explanation: The handbrake holds the car still when parked and helps prevent rolling back during a hill start.

questions.prompt: A red warning light stays on after you start the engine. What should you do?
options: Treat it as serious — do not drive until you know what it is
Carry on and have it checked when convenient
Ignore it if the car seems to drive normally
questions.explanation: Red means stop, amber means check. A red light — oil pressure, brakes, charging — can mean damage within minutes, so don't drive on it. The exception is the parking-brake light: that just means the handbrake is still on.

questions.prompt: You arrive at a four-way stop. Another vehicle has already stopped and is waiting. What must you do?
options: Stop, then go before the waiting vehicle if you are on its right
Stop, and let the vehicle that stopped first go before you
Slow down and go through if the way looks clear
questions.explanation: First to stop is first to go. Being on the right gives you nothing here — that yield-to-the-right habit belongs at a traffic circle, not at a four-way stop. Wait your turn in the order everyone arrived.

questions.prompt: What is the general following distance rule in good conditions?
options: Stay one vehicle length behind
Keep at least a two-second gap to the vehicle ahead
Always stay 100 m behind
questions.explanation: Pick a fixed point and count: you should reach it at least two seconds after the vehicle ahead, and leave more in the rain. No exact distance is written into the law — it asks you not to follow more closely than is reasonable, and two seconds is the standard that meets it.

questions.prompt: A single solid white no-overtaking line runs down the centre of the road. When may you cross it?
options: Whenever the road ahead is clear
Only to avoid an obstruction, and only when it is safe
To overtake a slow-moving vehicle
questions.explanation: A no-overtaking line (RM1) forbids overtaking, but you may cross it when you have to pass an obstruction in your lane and it is safe to do so. Do not confuse it with the double solid no-crossing line (RM2), which you may not cross at all.

questions.prompt: You approach a pedestrian crossing where people are already crossing on your half of the road. You should:
options: Speed up to pass before they reach you
Stop and allow them to finish crossing
Hoot to warn them to hurry
questions.explanation: Someone already on the crossing has the right of way, so stop and let them finish. Hooting at them or steering around them is both unlawful and dangerous.

questions.prompt: What should you do before changing lanes on a busy road?
options: Indicate, check your mirrors and your blind spot, then move when it is safe
Just indicate and move immediately
Move first, then indicate
questions.explanation: Signal your intention, check mirrors, then physically check the blind spot over your shoulder before moving. Mirrors alone miss the blind spot.

questions.prompt: You approach an eight-sided red sign. What must you do?
options: Slow down, and stop only if other vehicles are near
Come to a complete stop, then go when it is safe
Sound your hooter and continue
questions.explanation: An eight-sided (octagonal) red sign is always STOP. You must stop completely every time, then proceed only when the way is clear.

questions.prompt: A downward-pointing triangle with a red border means:
options: Stop
No entry
Yield / give way
questions.explanation: A downward triangle with a red border is a yield sign. Slow down and give right of way; only stop if something is coming.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a no-entry sign and a one-way sign?
options: They mean the same thing
No-entry forbids you from entering; one-way shows the permitted direction
One-way forbids you from entering; no-entry shows the direction
questions.explanation: A no-entry sign (red circle, white bar) forbids you from entering that road. A one-way sign (an arrow) simply shows the single direction traffic may travel.

questions.prompt: A red circle with the number 60 inside it tells you that:
options: The recommended speed is 60 km/h
You must drive at exactly 60 km/h
60 km/h is the maximum allowed
questions.explanation: A number in a red circle is a maximum speed limit. You may drive slower, but never faster than 60 km/h until another sign changes it.

questions.prompt: What tells the no-stopping sign apart from the no-parking sign?
options: No-stopping has two diagonal lines; no-parking has one
The letter inside: S for no stopping, P for no parking — both have one diagonal
No-stopping is a triangle; no-parking is a circle
questions.explanation: Both are red-ringed circles with a single diagonal, so the ring will not tell them apart — the letter will. P is no parking; S is no stopping. No stopping is the stricter of the two: you may not even pause to drop someone off.

questions.prompt: Unless a road sign shows otherwise, what is the general speed limit on a public road in an urban area?
options: 60 km/h
40 km/h
80 km/h
questions.explanation: The default urban speed limit in South Africa is 60 km/h. 40 km/h and 80 km/h are not the general urban default; a posted sign could set a different limit, but absent one the limit is 60.

questions.prompt: What is the general maximum speed limit for a light motor vehicle on a freeway, where no lower limit is posted?
options: 100 km/h
120 km/h
140 km/h
questions.explanation: The general freeway limit is 120 km/h. 100 km/h is the default for a non-freeway rural public road, and 140 km/h is not a legal South African limit.

questions.prompt: A goods vehicle with a gross vehicle mass over 9 000 kg is travelling on a freeway. What is the maximum speed it may legally travel?
options: 100 km/h
120 km/h
80 km/h
questions.explanation: A goods vehicle over 9 000 kg GVM is capped at 80 km/h even on a freeway, regardless of the 120 km/h general limit. The other options ignore the class-specific cap.

questions.prompt: In good conditions, what is the safest way to judge a following distance behind the vehicle ahead?
options: Keep a time gap of at least two seconds
Stay exactly 50 metres behind at all times
Keep one car length behind regardless of speed
questions.explanation: A time-based gap (the two-second rule) is correct because the safe distance grows automatically with speed. A fixed metre distance or 'one car length' does not scale with speed and is unsafe at higher speeds.

questions.prompt: At a four-way stop, what decides the order in which vehicles may go?
options: The larger or heavier vehicle goes first
The order in which they came to a stop
The vehicle going straight ahead goes first
questions.explanation: Vehicles proceed in the order they stopped — first to stop, first to go. Size and direction of travel do not create priority, and there is no main road at a four-way stop. The yield-to-the-right rule in regulation 301 is confined to junctions where traffic moves around a traffic island, so it does not decide this.

questions.prompt: What must you do when you approach a yield sign and the road you are joining is completely clear?
options: Come to a complete stop before proceeding
Sound your hooter and drive through
Slow down and proceed without stopping if it is safe
questions.explanation: A yield sign requires you to give way only if necessary; if the way is clear you may proceed without stopping. A complete stop is required at a stop sign, not a yield sign.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum legal blood-alcohol concentration for an ordinary (non-professional) driver in South Africa?
options: Below 0.05 g per 100 ml
Below 0.02 g per 100 ml
Below 0.08 g per 100 ml
questions.explanation: The ordinary-driver limit is below 0.05 g/100 ml. 0.02 applies to professional drivers, and 0.08 is the United States limit, not South Africa's.

questions.prompt: How close to a pedestrian crossing, on the approach side, may you NOT stop your vehicle?
options: Within 5 metres
Within 9 metres
Within 20 metres
questions.explanation: You may not stop within 9 metres on the approach to a pedestrian crossing. The 5-metre figure applies to parking near an intersection, a common point of confusion.

questions.prompt: Within what distance of an intersection may you NOT park in an urban area?
options: 9 metres
1.5 metres
5 metres
questions.explanation: You may not park within 5 metres of an intersection. 9 metres is the no-stopping distance before a pedestrian crossing, and 1.5 metres is the no-parking distance from a fire hydrant.

questions.prompt: Who must wear a seatbelt in a private car fitted with belts in all seats?
options: Every occupant, front and back
Only the driver
Only the front-seat occupants
questions.explanation: Every occupant of a seat fitted with a seatbelt must wear it. Limiting it to the driver or front seats is incorrect; the driver is also legally responsible for child passengers.

questions.prompt: An ambulance approaches from behind with its siren on. What should you do?
options: Speed up to stay ahead of it
Give it immediate right of way, moving left and stopping if needed
Maintain your speed and ignore it until it passes
questions.explanation: Emergency vehicles must be given immediate and absolute right of way — move to the left and stop if necessary. Speeding up or ignoring it obstructs an emergency response and is unlawful.

questions.prompt: After a collision that damaged another vehicle but injured no one, and you did not give your details to an officer at the scene, when must you report it?
options: Only if the other driver asks you to
There is no need to report a damage-only accident
To the police within 24 hours
questions.explanation: You must report an accident — including damage-only accidents — to the police within 24 hours if you did not give your details to an officer at the scene. Damage-only accidents are not exempt from reporting.

questions.prompt: Apart from between sunset and sunrise, when else must your headlights be switched on?
options: When persons or vehicles are not clearly visible at 150 metres
Only when another vehicle flashes you
Only inside tunnels
questions.explanation: Headlights must also be on whenever visibility drops so that persons or vehicles are not clearly visible at 150 metres — for example in fog or heavy rain. Waiting to be flashed or limiting it to tunnels is incorrect.

questions.prompt: There is a solid white line on your side of the road and a broken line on the oncoming side. May you overtake?
options: Yes, because there is a broken line on the road
No, you may not cross the solid line on your side
Yes, but only at night
questions.explanation: You obey the line nearest you. A solid line on your side is a no-crossing barrier, so you may not overtake — the broken line on the far side permits the oncoming traffic to cross, not you.

questions.prompt: A pedestrian is crossing on your half of the roadway at a pedestrian crossing. What must you do?
options: Sound your hooter so they hurry
Drive around behind them
Yield and let the pedestrian cross
questions.explanation: At a pedestrian crossing you must yield to a pedestrian on your half of the road. Hooting at or driving around a pedestrian on a crossing is unlawful and unsafe.

questions.prompt: A vehicle ahead of you has stopped at a pedestrian crossing. What may you NOT do?
options: Overtake the stopped vehicle
Wait behind it until it moves off
Check for pedestrians
questions.explanation: You may not overtake a vehicle that has stopped at a pedestrian crossing — a pedestrian you cannot see may be crossing in front of it. Waiting and checking for pedestrians are correct.

questions.prompt: Your indicators have failed. How do you signal a right turn by hand?
options: Right forearm pointing down
Right arm extended straight out, horizontal
Right forearm pointing up
questions.explanation: A right-turn hand signal is the right arm extended straight out horizontally. Forearm down signals a left turn; forearm up signals slowing or stopping.

questions.prompt: Which hand signal indicates that you intend to slow down or stop?
options: Right arm straight out horizontally
Right forearm pointing down
Right arm out, forearm pointing up, palm forward
questions.explanation: The slow-down/stop hand signal is the right arm out with the forearm pointing up, palm forward. Straight out means a right turn; forearm down means a left turn.

questions.prompt: You have just passed your learner's licence test. May you now drive alone on a public road?
options: No, you must always be supervised by a licensed driver
Yes, the learner's licence lets you drive alone
Yes, but only during the day
questions.explanation: A learner's licence does not permit driving alone. Regulation 99(2)(a) requires you to be under the direct personal supervision of someone seated next to you who holds a full licence for that class of vehicle. There is no L-plate requirement in South African law.

questions.prompt: What is the legal minimum tyre tread depth across the breadth of a tyre?
options: 5 mm
1 mm
10 mm
questions.explanation: The legal minimum tread is 1 mm across the breadth and around the full circumference. Below this the tyre is unroadworthy. 5 mm and 10 mm are well above the legal minimum.

questions.prompt: You normally keep a two-second following gap. What should you do when it is raining heavily?
options: Keep the same two-second gap
Halve the gap to keep up
At least double the time gap
questions.explanation: In rain or poor grip you should at least double the time gap (three to four seconds or more), because stopping distances lengthen on a wet road. Keeping or halving the gap is unsafe.

questions.prompt: You are approaching a traffic circle. Who has right of way?
options: Traffic already in the circle / approaching from your right
Whoever is the largest vehicle
You, because you are entering
questions.explanation: At a traffic circle you yield to traffic already circulating and approaching from your right. Vehicle size gives no priority, and an entering driver must give way, not take it.

questions.prompt: May you overtake when approaching the summit of a rise where you cannot see oncoming traffic?
options: Yes, if you are quick
No, overtaking is prohibited where visibility is restricted
Yes, if you sound your hooter
questions.explanation: Overtaking is prohibited approaching a rise, curve or any place where your view of oncoming traffic is restricted. Speed or hooting does not make it legal or safe.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum speed limit for a bus, or a minibus carrying passengers for reward, even on a freeway?
options: 120 km/h
140 km/h
100 km/h
questions.explanation: Regulation 293(1)(b) caps a bus, and a minibus used for the conveyance of persons for reward, at 100 km/h — below the 120 km/h general freeway limit. A privately used minibus is not covered by this cap and is on the general limits. 140 km/h is not a legal South African limit.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum legal blood-alcohol concentration for a professional (PrDP) driver?
options: Below 0.02 g per 100 ml
Below 0.05 g per 100 ml
Below 0.08 g per 100 ml
questions.explanation: Professional drivers face the stricter limit of below 0.02 g/100 ml. 0.05 is the ordinary-driver limit and 0.08 is the United States limit.

questions.prompt: How close to a fire hydrant may you NOT park?
options: Within 5 metres
Within 1.5 metres on either side
Within 9 metres
questions.explanation: You may not park within 1.5 metres either side of a fire hydrant. 5 metres is the no-parking distance from an intersection and 9 metres is the no-stopping distance before a pedestrian crossing.

questions.prompt: What is the general speed limit on a public road outside an urban area that is not a freeway?
options: 60 km/h
120 km/h
100 km/h
questions.explanation: The default limit on a non-freeway rural public road is 100 km/h. 60 is the urban default and 120 is the freeway limit.

questions.prompt: Your braking (stopping) distance becomes longer when:
options: The road is wet, your speed is higher, or the vehicle is loaded
Only when it is dark
Only when the tyres are new
questions.explanation: Stopping distance increases on a wet road, at higher speed and when the vehicle is laden — all three. Darkness and new tyres are not the primary factors.

questions.prompt: A child under the age of three is travelling in a private car. How must the child be secured?
options: On an adult's lap with the adult belted
In an appropriate child restraint (car seat)
With an ordinary adult seatbelt
questions.explanation: A child under three is an "infant" and must travel in an appropriate child restraint — regulation 213(6A), added in 2014. An adult's lap is not a restraint, and an adult seatbelt does not fit an infant safely. The requirement does not apply on a minibus, midibus or bus operating for reward.

questions.prompt: In which situation may you lawfully pass another vehicle on its left?
options: Never — you must always pass on the right
Whenever the left lane is empty on the open road
When the vehicle ahead is signalling and turning right
questions.explanation: You may pass on the left when the vehicle ahead is signalling and turning right (also in a one-way street or in multi-lane traffic in your direction). 'Never' is wrong, and casually undertaking on the open road is not permitted.

questions.prompt: An ordinary driver's breath-alcohol concentration must be below which limit?
options: 0.24 mg per 1 000 ml
0.50 mg per 1 000 ml
0.80 mg per 1 000 ml
questions.explanation: The ordinary-driver breath limit is below 0.24 mg per 1 000 ml. The other figures are not the legal breath limit; professional drivers face a stricter 0.10.

questions.prompt: You are following closely behind another vehicle at night. What should your headlights be on?
options: Bright (main) beam to see further
Dipped (low) beam so you do not dazzle the driver ahead
Switched off to save the battery
questions.explanation: Use dipped beam when following closely so you do not dazzle the driver ahead through their mirrors. Regulation 157(3) expressly requires you to dip for oncoming traffic; dipping when following is the same courtesy and is what the test expects. Driving at night without lights is unlawful under regulation 157(1)(b).

questions.prompt: What must every vehicle do on arriving at a four-way stop?
options: Slow down and proceed if clear
Yield only to vehicles on the main road
Come to a complete stop, then go in order of arrival
questions.explanation: Every vehicle must come to a complete stop, then proceed in the order the vehicles stopped — first to stop, first to go. There is no main road at a four-way stop. Note that the yield-to-the-right rule in regulation 301 applies where traffic moves around a traffic island, not here.

questions.prompt: After an accident, to whom must you give your name, address and vehicle details?
options: To anyone with reasonable grounds to ask, e.g. the other driver
Only to the police, never to other people
To nobody — it is private information
questions.explanation: You must give your details to anyone with reasonable grounds for requiring them, such as the other driver or an injured party, and report to police within 24 hours if you did not give details to an officer at the scene.

questions.prompt: You want to tow a trailer with a gross mass over 750 kg behind a light motor vehicle. Which licence code do you need?
options: Code A
Code EB
Code C
questions.explanation: Towing a trailer over 750 kg behind a light motor vehicle requires Code EB. Code A is for motorcycles; Code C is a bus or goods vehicle whose gross vehicle mass exceeds 16 000 kg — the 3 500 kg to 16 000 kg band is Code C1.

questions.prompt: It is an offence to drive while under the influence of:
options: Alcohol only
Prescription medicine can never be an offence
Alcohol or any drug having a narcotic effect
questions.explanation: Section 65 makes it an offence to drive under the influence of alcohol OR any drug having a narcotic effect — including some prescription medicines that impair driving. It is not limited to alcohol.

questions.prompt: You stop at a four-way stop. A moment later a bakkie coming from your right also comes to a complete stop. Who may move off first?
options: The bakkie, because a vehicle on your right always has right of way
You, because you stopped first
Whoever is going straight rather than turning
questions.explanation: At a four-way stop the order is decided by who stopped first: sign R1.4 says you may not move into the junction until every vehicle that stopped at another stop line before you, and that would in the normal course of events cross your path, has cleared the junction. You stopped first, so you go. There is no yield-to-the-right tie-breaker at a four-way stop — reg 301 is written only for a junction where traffic has to move around a traffic island — and going straight rather than turning gives you nothing.

questions.prompt: You are following a car on a dry, clear road. It passes a lamp post, you start counting, and you reach the same lamp post after about one second. What should you do?
options: Nothing — one second is enough on a dry road
Speed up and overtake so you are not stuck behind it
Ease off until the gap is at least two seconds
questions.explanation: Two seconds is the minimum gap in good conditions, so a one-second gap is too close and you must drop back. One second is not enough on any road surface, and overtaking to escape a gap you created yourself just moves the problem instead of fixing it.

questions.prompt: The car ahead of you has stopped at a pedestrian crossing to let people walk across. The lane next to you looks clear. What may you do?
options: Stay and stop behind it — you may not pass a vehicle that has stopped at a pedestrian crossing
Pass it on the right, as long as you can see your side of the crossing is clear
Hoot to warn the pedestrians, then pass slowly
questions.explanation: A vehicle stopped at a crossing hides pedestrians from you, so the law simply does not allow you to pass it. Checking 'your side' is worthless when the stopped car is blocking your view of someone still walking, and hooting pressures pedestrians instead of protecting them.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of checks before you change lanes?
options: Signal, then check your rear view mirror, check your side mirror, check your blind spot, then move
Check your rear view mirror, check your side mirror, signal, check your blind spot, then move
Check your blind spot, check your side mirror, check your rear view mirror,  move, then signal
questions.explanation: Mirror, signal, blind spot, move — you gather information first, then tell others, then take one last look for what the mirrors missed. Signalling before you have looked commits you before you know it is safe, and signalling after you have already moved warns nobody.

questions.prompt: You check your mirrors before changing lanes and they are clear. Why must you still look over your shoulder?
options: To show the examiner that you are alert
To check that your indicator is actually flashing
Because a vehicle can sit in the blind spot your mirrors do not cover
questions.explanation: Mirrors leave a blind spot alongside and slightly behind you that is big enough to hide a motorcycle or a whole car, which is exactly what the over-the-shoulder look catches. It is a real safety check, not a performance for the examiner, and your indicator is confirmed on the dashboard, not over your shoulder.

questions.prompt: You have finished changing lanes and your indicator is still flashing. What should you do?
options: Cancel it as soon as the lane change is done
Leave it on until you next turn
Leave it on — it warns drivers behind that you have just moved
questions.explanation: An indicator left running tells other drivers you are about to move again, so cancel it the moment the manoeuvre is complete. Leaving it on until your next turn, or as a 'warning', feeds everyone around you false information about what you plan to do.

questions.prompt: You signal in good time to pull out into the next lane. Does the signal give you the right to move across?
options: Yes — once you have signalled, other drivers must let you in
No — a signal only announces your intention, so you still have to make sure the lane is clear
Yes, provided you have signalled for at least three seconds
questions.explanation: A signal warns others what you plan to do; it never creates right of way, so the mirror and blind-spot checks still decide whether you may move. There is also no magic number of seconds that turns a signal into permission — the law asks only that it is clear and early enough to warn.

questions.prompt: You are approaching a mini-circle and a car is already travelling around it. What must you do?
options: Enter the circle first if you get there before it finishes its turn
Stop completely and wait for every vehicle at the circle to leave
Give way to the vehicle already travelling around the mini-circle and only enter when it is safe to do so
questions.explanation: A mini-circle is controlled by sign R2.2, and R2.2 decides priority by the yield line: you must give way to any vehicle that will cross a yield line at the junction before you and whose path will cross yours. A car already travelling around the circle crossed its yield line before you did, so you wait for a safe gap and then enter, moving clockwise. Pushing in ahead of it takes a gap that is not yours, and waiting for the circle to empty completely is not required and simply blocks everyone behind you.

questions.prompt: Two cars reach a mini-circle at about the same time. What decides which one has right of way?
options: Whichever car crosses the yield line first
The car approaching from the right, always
Whichever car is going straight through rather than turning
questions.explanation: A mini-circle is controlled by sign R2.2, and R2.2 decides it by the yield line: you give way to any vehicle that will cross a yield line at the junction before you and whose path will cross yours. It is not a yield-to-the-right rule. That rule lives in reg 301, which is written for a junction where traffic must move around a traffic island and which expressly gives way to a contrary road traffic sign — and R2.2 is exactly such a sign. What a driver intends to do after the circle makes no difference either. Once you are in, keep moving clockwise and try not to encroach on the circle itself.

questions.prompt: You reach a mini-circle in a quiet suburb and there is no other traffic anywhere near it. What must you do?
options: Come to a complete stop, the same as you would at a four-way stop
Slow down, make sure it is safe, and drive around the mini-circle without stopping unnecessarily.
Drive through at your normal speed, since a yield sign only binds you when other traffic is actually there
questions.explanation: Sign R2.2 asks you to yield, not to stop, so with nothing approaching you slow down, check the other entrances and keep moving. A full stop is what a stop sign demands, and R2.2 is not a stop sign — it is used with yield line RTM2, not stop line RTM1. Holding your normal speed is the real fault: yielding means being able to give way to a vehicle that crosses a yield line before you do, and at full speed you cannot.

questions.prompt: You are driving around a mini-circle and the next exit is the one you want to take. What should you do?
options: Nothing — indicators are not used inside a circle
Signal only once you have left the circle
Signal before the exit so other drivers know you are leaving the circle
questions.explanation: Drivers waiting to enter need to know you are coming out, so you signal before the exit while the message can still change what they do. Not signalling at all leaves them guessing, and signalling once you are already out is too late to be any use to anyone.

questions.prompt: The robot ahead of you turns green. What does this allow you to do?
options: Proceed immediately — a green light guarantees you the right of way
Scan the intersection and proceed only once the way is clear
You must proceed; stopping while the light is green is not permitted
questions.explanation: Green is permission to go only when the way ahead is actually clear, so you still scan the intersection before moving. It does not guarantee that cross traffic has stopped, and it never forces you to move into a situation that is unsafe.

questions.prompt: You are approaching a robot at speed and the light changes to amber when you are only about a car's length from the stop line. Stopping would need violent braking, and there is a vehicle close behind you. What should you do?
options: Brake as hard as you can and stop before the line
Accelerate to clear the intersection before the light turns red
Proceed through intersection with caution, because you cannot stop safely
questions.explanation: A steady amber (yellow) disc means stop behind the stop line RTM1 — but it carries an express proviso: if you are so close when it is displayed that you cannot stop safely, you may proceed with caution against it. 'With caution' is the legal standard, and it is not the same as carrying on at whatever speed you happened to be doing. Emergency braking invites the car behind into your boot, and accelerating to beat the light is exactly the fault the examiner is watching for.

questions.prompt: Your light is green, but traffic on the far side of the intersection is backed up and there is no space for your car to come out the other side. What should you do?
options: Enter the intersection and wait there — the green light gives you the right to be in it
Wait behind the stop line before entering the intersection until there is enough space to clear it completely.
Enter as long as you can stop with your rear bumper clear of the stop line
questions.explanation: Green only lets you go when the way is clear, and it is not clear if you would come to a standstill inside the intersection and block the cross traffic. Neither the green light nor keeping your bumper past the line gives you permission to obstruct the intersection.

questions.prompt: The robot ahead turns red as you approach. Where must your vehicle come to a stop?
options: Behind the stop line
With your front wheels resting on the stop line so you can still see the light
Far enough forward to be level with the traffic light itself
questions.explanation: Red means stop behind the line — the space in front of it belongs to pedestrians and crossing traffic. Creeping onto the line or up to the signal head puts your car where other road users need to be, and counts as crossing the line on red.

questions.prompt: The light turns amber while you are still several car lengths back. You could stop before the line, but it would take firm braking. Nothing is following you closely. What does the rule require?
options: Carry on through — you are too close to stop comfortably
Brake firmly but under control and stop behind the line
Carry on through, because braking firmly on amber is never safe
questions.explanation: Amber asks whether you can stop safely, not whether it would be comfortable — with a clear road behind you, controlled firm braking is safe, so you stop. Only when a safe stop is genuinely impossible may you continue through.

questions.prompt: You need to pull over for a moment to drop a friend off in a busy street. Which of these places may you legally stop?
options: Right on the pedestrian crossing, with your hazard lights on
In a marked bay in the side street, well clear of the corner
Just around the corner of the intersection, with two wheels on the pavement
questions.explanation: A marked bay clear of the corner is the only choice that neither blocks traffic nor sits on or near a crossing or intersection. Hazard lights do not make an illegal stop legal, and stopping right at an intersection hides you and your passengers from approaching drivers.

questions.prompt: In good, dry conditions you keep a two-second gap to the vehicle in front. What should that gap become in heavy rain?
options: Four seconds or more
Still two seconds — the gap does not change with the weather
Three second, so you stay close enough to see the vehicle's brake lights
questions.explanation: On a wet road it takes you much longer to pull up, so the two-second gap is stretched to four seconds or more. Keeping the same gap ignores the longer stopping distance, and closing up to one second leaves you no room at all to react.

questions.prompt: Thick fog rolls in and visibility drops sharply. Apart from slowing down, what should you do?
options: Put your hazard lights on and keep your normal speed
Switch your headlights on and increase your following distance
Tuck in close behind the vehicle ahead and follow its tail lights
questions.explanation: Headlights make you visible to others and a longer gap buys you time when you can only see a short way ahead. Hazard lights at normal speed still leave you arriving too fast to stop, and following someone's tail lights closely means you inherit their crash.

questions.prompt: You are on a road signposted 100 km/h. It is raining steadily and the light is fading. May you drive at 100 km/h?
options: Yes — the sign sets the speed you are expected to drive
Yes, as long as your headlights are on
No — the sign is a maximum for good conditions, so drop your speed to suit the wet road and poor light
questions.explanation: A speed limit is a ceiling for good conditions, not a target, and rain plus poor light means you need to be slower than the sign allows. Treating the number as the expected speed, or thinking headlights cancel out the loss of grip, is how learners lose control in the wet.

questions.prompt: Why exactly does a wet or slippery road force you to leave a bigger following gap?
options: Your tyres have less grip on a wet or slippery road, your braking distance is longer, so you need more space to stop safely.
Your reaction time gets slower when it rains and your tyres have less grip on a wet or slippery road
Vehicles ahead of you brake harder in the wet
questions.explanation: Rain changes the braking part of the equation — with less grip the car travels further after you hit the brakes, so you need more space in hand. Your reaction time is set by you, not the weather, and there is no rule that says the car ahead brakes harder in the wet.

questions.prompt: In which of these situations may you legally be out of your seatbelt while the vehicle is moving?
options: While you are reversing or moving into or out of a parking bay
While you are driving slowly in a quiet residential street
While you are the front passenger on a very short trip
questions.explanation: Reg 213(4) requires an adult occupying a seat fitted with a seatbelt to wear it, and carries an express proviso that it does not apply while reversing or moving in or out of a parking bay or area — that is the exception in the question, and it exists because the belt stops you turning to see behind you. A low speed or a short trip changes nothing. Two things the old wording got wrong are worth knowing: the duty in reg 213(4) is written for adults (over 14 years, or 1,5 m and taller), with children covered separately by reg 213(6) and (7); and the parking-bay proviso is not the only exception, because an MEC may exempt a person on medical grounds under reg 213(9).

questions.prompt: You are giving a five-year-old a lift and there is no child seat in your car. What must happen?
options: He must wear the seatbelt fitted to that seat
He may travel unrestrained, because no child restraint is available
He must share an adult's seatbelt on that adult's lap
questions.explanation: A child uses a child restraint when one is available, and a seatbelt when one is not — so the belt goes on. Leaving him loose is never allowed, and two people in one belt means the adult's weight is thrown onto the child in a crash.

questions.prompt: You are out practising on your learner's licence. Where must the licence itself be?
options: Left at home in a safe place, as long as you can quote the number
With you in the vehicle every time you drive
Only needed once you book your driving test
questions.explanation: You may drive only under the authority and conditions of your licence, and you must keep that licence with you in the vehicle. Quoting the number is not the same as carrying it, and it is required on every drive, not just on test day.

questions.prompt: You hold a learner's licence for a light motor vehicle. Which of these people may legally supervise you?
options: A friend who also holds a learner's licence for the same class
Any adult over 21 who is sitting in the car with you
A driver who holds a full driving licence for that class of vehicle
questions.explanation: Your supervisor must hold a full driving licence for the class you are driving, and must sit next to you — or immediately behind you where there is no seat alongside. Another learner holds no full licence to supervise with, and being an adult means nothing on its own.

questions.prompt: You hold a learner's licence for a motorcycle. May you take a friend on the back?
options: Yes, as long as the friend wears a helmet
Yes, as long as you stay off busy roads
No — a motorcycle learner may not carry a passenger
questions.explanation: A motorcycle learner may not carry a passenger at all. A helmet protects the passenger but does not make carrying one lawful, and the restriction applies on every public road, quiet or busy.

questions.prompt: Thabo wants a learner's licence for a light motor vehicle. What is the minimum age, and how long will that licence stay valid?
options: 17 years old, and it stays valid for 24 months
18 years old, and it stays valid for 24 months
17 years old, and it stays valid for 12 months
questions.explanation: A light motor vehicle learner's licence may be obtained at 17, and is valid for 24 months. The 24-month period comes from a 2010 ministerial notice: regulation 101(1) itself still reads 18 months, and General Notice 134 of 17 February 2010 extended it. Each wrong option changes exactly one of the two figures.

questions.prompt: When may you legally use your vehicle's hooter on a public road?
options: Whenever you want to greet someone you recognise
Only where the traffic regulations require it, or on the grounds of safety
At any time between sunrise and sunset
questions.explanation: The hooter may only be sounded where a traffic regulation requires it or where safety demands it. Greeting someone is not a safety reason, and there is no daytime exemption — the time of day makes no difference to the rule.

questions.prompt: A driver sits outside a block of flats late at night revving his engine hard and hooting repeatedly. Besides misusing the hooter, what else has he done wrong?
options: Nothing else — noise is a nuisance but not a traffic offence
Nothing under traffic law; only a municipal by-law could apply
He has committed the separate offence of operating a vehicle so that it makes excessive avoidable noise
questions.explanation: Making excessive avoidable noise with a vehicle is an offence in its own right, separate from the hooter rule. It is not merely a nuisance, and it does not depend on a local by-law to be unlawful.

questions.prompt: You pull up outside a friend's house and hoot twice to let them know you have arrived. Is this allowed?
options: No — the hooter may only be used where a regulation requires it or for safety
Yes, two short taps are always acceptable
Yes, as long as it is before 21:00
questions.explanation: Calling someone out of a house is not a safety reason, so it is unlawful use of the hooter. Keeping the taps short or hooting early in the evening does not create an exception — only a regulation or a genuine safety need does.

questions.prompt: A car in the next lane starts drifting across the line towards your door. What is the correct use of the hooter here?
options: Hold the hooter down until the other driver moves back across
Do not hoot at all — hooting is never allowed on a public road
Give one short tap to warn the driver, then get back to steering, braking and looking
questions.explanation: This is a real safety warning, so a short tap is lawful — and then your hands and eyes belong back on the driving. Leaning on the hooter adds noise without adding information, and hooting is not banned outright, only limited to regulation and safety use.

questions.prompt: Which one of these is a lawful use of the hooter?
options: Warning a pedestrian who is stepping off the kerb into your path
Telling the driver in front of you that the robot has turned green
Showing your annoyance at a driver who cut in front of you
questions.explanation: Only the first is a warning of actual danger, which is the safety ground the regulation allows. Impatience at a green light and anger at another driver are common but are not safety reasons, so both are unlawful uses.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum legal tread depth for a tyre used on a public road?
options: 1.6 mm
1 mm
2 mm
questions.explanation: The tread pattern must be at least 1 mm deep, clearly visible across the tyre's full breadth and around its whole circumference. 1.6 mm and 2mm are safer depths to aim for, but neither is the legal minimum you will be tested on.

questions.prompt: You check a tyre and find the rubber is now worn level with the raised tread-wear bar inside the groove. What does that tell you?
options: The tyre is illegal and must be replaced
The tyre is still fine until the bar itself starts wearing away
The tyre is still fine as long as the sidewall has no cracks
questions.explanation: A tyre is illegal the moment the tread is worn level with its tread-wear indicator — that is exactly what the bar is built in to show. Waiting for the bar to wear down, or checking only the sidewall, both leave you driving on an illegal tyre.

questions.prompt: Before a trip you find a lump bulging out of one tyre's sidewall, although the tread on that tyre is still deep. What must you do?
options: Nothing — tread depth is what the law measures
Let some air out to take the strain off the lump
Replace the tyre, because a lump or bulge makes it illegal
questions.explanation: A lump or bulge makes a tyre illegal on its own, no matter how good the tread still is. Dropping the pressure does not repair a damaged casing — it just changes how the tyre handles.

questions.prompt: The outer half of your front tyre still has deep tread, but the inner edge is worn smooth and the cords are showing. Is that tyre legal?
options: Yes — most of the tread is still there
No — the tread must show across the tyre's full breadth, and showing cords makes it illegal anyway
Yes, provided you keep your speed down
questions.explanation: The tread pattern must be clearly visible across the full breadth of the tyre and around its whole circumference, so a bald inner edge fails on its own — and exposed cords are a separate reason the tyre is illegal. Driving slower does not make an illegal tyre legal.

questions.prompt: Where must a vehicle's licence disc be displayed?
options: On the lower left of the windscreen, so it can be read from outside
Anywhere on the dashboard, as long as you can produce it when asked
On the inside of the driver's door
questions.explanation: The disc goes on the lower left of the windscreen precisely so it can be read from outside the vehicle. Lying loose on the dashboard or hidden in the door, it cannot be read where the law requires it to be.

questions.prompt: How must number plates be fitted to a car on a public road?
options: One plate at the back only
One at the front and one at the back, both fully visible and clearly legible
One at the front only, unless you are towing something
questions.explanation: A number plate is required at both the front and the back of a car, and each must be affixed so that every letter and figure is clearly legible and the whole plate is clearly visible. A single plate leaves the vehicle unidentifiable from the other direction. Towing does not let you drop either plate — but it does relax one thing, which is why the third option is a trap worth understanding: reg 35(9) disapplies the legibility and visibility requirements for the REAR plate while a motor vehicle is towing another vehicle.

questions.prompt: You fit a dark smoked cover over your rear number plate because you think it looks better. What is the legal position?
options: Allowed, because the plate is still there underneath the cover
Allowed at night, since plates are hard to read in the dark anyway
Not allowed — a number plate may not be obscured and must stay clearly legible
questions.explanation: A plate must be fully visible and clearly legible, so anything that obscures it is an offence even though the plate is physically fitted. Darkness does not suspend the rule either — the plate must be readable at night too.

questions.prompt: Your licence disc is valid for another eight months, but one headlamp has failed and the brakes are badly worn. May you keep driving the car?
options: Yes — a valid disc is what the law checks
No — the car must also be in a roadworthy condition, not just registered and licensed
Yes, as long as you only drive during the day
questions.explanation: You may only drive a car that is registered, licensed and roadworthy, and a valid disc says nothing about the state of the brakes or lights. Driving only by day does not repair a worn brake, so the car stays unroadworthy.

questions.prompt: Which statement about driving a car on a public road is correct?
options: A valid licence disc makes the car legal to drive
A car in perfect mechanical condition may be driven even if it has never been registered
The car must be registered, licensed and in a roadworthy condition
questions.explanation: All three requirements apply together — registered, licensed and roadworthy. A disc alone only proves the licence fee is paid, and good mechanical condition is no substitute for being registered.

questions.prompt: You hold a Code B licence. What is the heaviest trailer you may tow behind a light motor vehicle?
options: A trailer with a gross vehicle mass of 750 kg or less
A trailer with a gross vehicle mass of 1 500 kg or less
Any trailer, as long as the car is powerful enough to pull it
questions.explanation: Code B covers a light vehicle plus a trailer of 750 kg gross vehicle mass or less; anything heavier needs Code EB. What the car can physically pull has nothing to do with what your licence allows.

questions.prompt: Your family's caravan has a gross vehicle mass of 1 200 kg and you hold a Code B licence. What must you do before you may tow it?
options: Nothing — Code B covers any trailer behind a light vehicle
Obtain a Code EB licence, because the trailer is over 750 kg GVM
Fit heavier-duty tyres to the towing car
questions.explanation: Once a trailer behind a light vehicle exceeds 750 kg GVM you need a Code EB licence. Code B does not stretch to cover it, and changing the towing car's tyres does not change what your licence permits.

questions.prompt: You are driving a car and towing a light trailer. Do the normal speed limits change?
options: No — the normal speed limits still apply to you
Yes, you may go 20 km/h faster to keep the trailer stable
Yes, the limit falls away once you are on a freeway
questions.explanation: Towing gives a car no special speed allowance — the general limits in reg 292 apply exactly as they would without the trailer, and both wrong options invent an exemption that does not exist. Heavier combinations are a different story, which is why the question is about a car: reg 293(1)(a) puts a goods vehicle or combination over 9 000 kg on 80 km/h, and reg 295(1) puts a tractor and its trailer on 35 km/h.

questions.prompt: An empty box trailer is light enough to push by hand, but the plate on it shows a gross vehicle mass of 1 000 kg. Which licence do you need to tow it behind a light motor vehicle?
options: Code B, because the trailer is empty and light right now
Either code, as long as you drive slowly
Code EB, because the trailer's plated gross vehicle mass is over 750 kg
questions.explanation: The licence code is decided by the gross vehicle mass shown on the trailer's own plate, not by how heavy it happens to be on the day, so 1 000 kg GVM puts it into Code EB. Driving slowly changes nothing about which licence you need.

questions.prompt: Apart from between sunset and sunrise, when must your headlamps, rear lamps and number plate lamps be lit?
options: Whenever poor light or bad weather means people and vehicles are not clearly visible at 150 metres
Only when the rain is heavy enough to need your wipers
Only when you are inside a tunnel
questions.explanation: The second trigger is visibility: if people and vehicles are not clearly visible at 150 m, your lamps go on, whatever the cause. Tying the rule to your wipers or to tunnels would leave you driving unlit in fog, dust or smoke. A motorcycle's headlamp must be lit at all times while it is being ridden on a public road.

questions.prompt: You are on a dark road with your main beam on when a car appears coming towards you. What must you do?
options: Leave the main beam on so the other driver can see your car clearly
Dip your headlights to low beam before the oncoming vehicle is dazzled
Switch all your lights off until the car has passed
questions.explanation: You must switch off the main beam whenever it could dangerously dazzle oncoming traffic; your dipped lamps still keep you visible. Leaving the main beam on blinds the other driver, and switching everything off makes you invisible and breaks the rule on lamps being lit after sunset.

questions.prompt: You are on a normal two-way road and want to get past a slower car travelling in the same direction as you. On which side of that car must you pass?
options: On its left
On its right
On whichever side has the most space at the time
questions.explanation: The rule is keep left, pass right: you move out to the right of the vehicle ahead, pass at a safe distance, and return to the left once you are safely clear. That is the default in reg 298(1), and on the ordinary two-way road in the question the right is the side. Passing on the left is not always unlawful — reg 298(1) carries provisos that permit it, for instance when the vehicle ahead has signalled that it is turning right — but 'whichever side has the most space' is not one of them, and no proviso ever lets you pass on the shoulder or the verge.

questions.prompt: A slow truck is holding you up on a single-lane road. There is a wide surfaced shoulder to the left of the yellow line. What may you legally do?
options: Move onto the shoulder and pass the truck on its left
Stay in your lane and wait until it is safe to pass on the truck's right
Straddle the yellow line so you are half on the shoulder and half in the lane
questions.explanation: The shoulder is not an overtaking lane — you may not drive on the shoulder or the verge to get past, so both the shoulder options are wrong. The only legal overtake here is out to the right when it is safe, then back left once you are clear of the truck.

questions.prompt: You have pulled out to the right and are overtaking another vehicle. When may you move back into the left lane?
options: As soon as your car is alongside the other vehicle's cab
The moment your front bumper is ahead of its front bumper
Only once you are safely clear of the vehicle you have passed
questions.explanation: You return to the left only when you are safely clear — far enough ahead that you are not cutting the other driver off. Being alongside means you are still beside the vehicle, and being a bumper ahead still puts your rear across its front, which is exactly how overtaking crashes happen.

questions.prompt: On a two-way road, when may you drive on the right-hand half of the roadway?
options: Briefly, when it is safe, no sign forbids it, or a sign or traffic officer directs you
Whenever the left-hand side has potholes you would rather avoid
At any time after dark, when there is less oncoming traffic
questions.explanation: Encroaching on the right half is allowed only as a short, safe exception — such as overtaking — or when a road sign or an officer sends you there. Avoiding potholes and driving at night are not exceptions; the keep-left rule applies just as strongly in the dark, when you can see oncoming traffic least well.

questions.prompt: In which one of these situations may a driver legally pass another vehicle on its left?
options: On any road, if the vehicle ahead is driving well below the speed limit
On a two-way road, if there is a wide shoulder marked off by a yellow line
On a one-way roadway with marked traffic lanes
questions.explanation: Of the three situations offered, only the one-way roadway divided into marked traffic lanes is permitted — that is proviso (d) to reg 298(1). A driver going below the speed limit creates no right to undertake, and a shoulder is never an overtaking lane: reg 298(1)'s further proviso bars any of the left-passing cases from being done on the shoulder or the verge. Note that reg 298(1) does allow passing on the left in other circumstances too — when the vehicle ahead has signalled a right turn, and on wide urban roads — so this is the only lawful case here, not the only one in law.

questions.prompt: You realise the vehicle behind you wants to pass. What does the law require you to do?
options: Move as near to the left edge of the roadway as you safely can, and do not accelerate
Hold your exact position and speed so the other driver knows what to expect
Accelerate so that you pull away and the other driver no longer needs to pass
questions.explanation: The driver being passed has a positive duty: ease left where it is safe and keep your speed steady until they are through. Holding position ignores that duty, and accelerating is the classic mistake — it strands the overtaking driver on the wrong side of the road for longer.

questions.prompt: You are in the right-hand lane of a freeway when the car behind you flashes its headlights at you. What does this mean and what should you do?
options: It is an insult and you should ignore it and keep your line
It warns you that your lights are faulty, so you should stop as soon as possible
It is the legal way for that driver to say they are coming past, so if it is safe move into a lane on your left and keep your speed steady
questions.explanation: On a freeway, reg 323(6) makes flashing the headlights the recognised way for a following driver to signal that they intend to overtake, and reg 323(5) then requires you — as the driver in the right-hand lane — to move into a lane on your left, when you can do so without endangering anyone, and not to accelerate until that vehicle has passed. Treating it as rudeness leaves the other driver stuck on your right, and stopping for a 'faulty light' invents a message the signal does not carry. Off the freeway, reg 298(3) imposes the same duty to move as near to the left edge as you safely can and not accelerate.

questions.prompt: A car is halfway through overtaking you when you notice you are now below the speed limit. What are you allowed to do?
options: Speed up to the limit, because you are entitled to use the full legal speed
Keep your speed steady until the other vehicle has completely passed you
Brake hard so the other driver can get past faster
questions.explanation: You may not accelerate until the overtaking vehicle has passed — the speed limit is a maximum you are allowed, not something you are entitled to reclaim mid-overtake. Braking hard is also wrong: a sudden change in your speed is unpredictable and can pull the other driver into danger just as badly.

questions.prompt: You are travelling in the right-hand lane of a freeway when a faster vehicle comes up close behind you. What must you do?
options: If it is safe, move into a lane on your left so the vehicle can pass
Stay where you are, since you are already at the speed limit
If it is safe, move further right onto the shoulder next to the barrier
questions.explanation: In the freeway's right-hand lane you are required to move into a lane on your left when a vehicle behind wants to pass. Being at the limit yourself gives you no right to sit in the right lane, and there is no legal move further right — the shoulder is not a driving lane.

questions.prompt: Before you ease left to let a following vehicle pass, what must you check first?
options: Nothing — you are required to move left immediately
Only your speedometer, to make sure you are under the limit
Check your mirrors, your blind spot, and make sure the left lane is clear before moving over
questions.explanation: The duty is to move as near to the left as you can do so safely, which means checking your mirrors and the space on your left before moving. Swerving left without looking can put you into a cyclist, a pedestrian or a broken-down vehicle, and your speedometer tells you nothing about whether that space is clear.

questions.prompt: A road is split into two roadways by a grass median. Which roadway may you drive on?
options: Either one, as long as you stay on the left side of that roadway
The left-hand roadway, unless a sign or a traffic officer directs you onto another one
The right-hand roadway, because it is the faster one
questions.explanation: On a divided road you are restricted to the left-hand roadway; only a road sign or a traffic officer can send you onto a different one. 'Either one' ignores that restriction completely, and there is no rule that makes a right-hand roadway a legal choice for the sake of speed.

questions.prompt: You are on a dual carriageway and you realise you have driven past your turn-off. What is the correct thing to do?
options: Carry on to the next legal crossing or interchange and come back from there
Cross the median as soon as there is a gap in the oncoming traffic
Reverse along the left edge of the roadway until you reach the turn-off
questions.explanation: Missing a turn costs you a few minutes, not a shortcut: you carry on to the next constructed intersection or interchange and turn around there. Cutting through the median is prohibited by reg 297(2) no matter how clear the road looks. Reversing is worse than it sounds — reg 308(1)(a) permits a vehicle to travel backwards only when it can be done in safety and only for as long as is necessary, and on a dual carriageway you would be reversing into traffic coming up behind you at full speed.

questions.prompt: What may you do with the dividing section (the median) that separates two roadways?
options: Drive along it when the roadway is congested
Park on it while you wait for a passenger
Nothing, except to cross it through a constructed intersection
questions.explanation: Reg 297(2) prohibits driving on, over, across or within the dividing section, with one exception: you may cross it through a constructed intersection — and not even there if a road traffic sign or a traffic officer forbids it. Driving along it to skip congestion and stopping on it to wait are both outside that exception, and both put you in the one strip of road that other drivers never expect to find a vehicle in.

questions.prompt: On a divided road, what is the only lawful way to get from the left-hand roadway across to the other roadway?
options: Across the dividing section, provided both roadways are clear and you do it quickly
Through a properly built intersection — and not even there if a sign or a traffic officer forbids it
Across the dividing section, provided you switch on your hazard lights first
questions.explanation: The crossing must happen at a proper intersection built for it, and even that can be closed to you by a sign or an officer's direction. A clear road does not make crossing the median legal, and hazard lights are a warning device, not a permission slip.

questions.prompt: You are waiting at the end of a side street to join a busy dual carriageway. When may you enter the roadway?
options: Only when you can do it without endangering other traffic
As soon as the nearest vehicle flashes its lights at you
Whenever you have waited longer than the drivers already on the roadway
questions.explanation: Entering a roadway is only allowed when you can do so without endangering traffic already on it — the judgement is yours and the responsibility stays with you. Another driver's flash is a courtesy that cannot make an unsafe gap safe, and time spent waiting gives you no right of way at all.

questions.prompt: Which of these may NOT be operated on a freeway?
options: A bicycle & electric motorcycles
A light delivery vehicle
A minibus carrying passengers
questions.explanation: Bicycles are on the banned list for freeways, along with animal-drawn vehicles, tractors, motor tricycles and quadrucycles, and small or electric motorcycles. A light delivery vehicle and a minibus are ordinary motor vehicles and are not on that list.

questions.prompt: A rider wants to take a 50 cc scooter onto the freeway to shorten the trip. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, as long as the scooter can keep up with the traffic
No — a motorcycle of 50 cc or less may not be operated on a freeway
Yes, but only in the left-hand lane
questions.explanation: Motorcycles of 50 cc or less, and electrically driven motorcycles, are on the list of vehicles banned from freeways, so the trip is illegal no matter how it is ridden. Keeping up with traffic and staying left are both irrelevant — the ban is on the vehicle itself, not on how you use it.

questions.prompt: You are driving on a freeway and your passenger asks you to pull over on the shoulder so they can take a photo of the view. What must you do?
options: Stop briefly on the shoulder with your hazard lights on
Stop, but only if you keep it under two minutes
Keep driving — you may not stop on a freeway for that reason
questions.explanation: Stopping on a freeway is only allowed where a sign or a traffic officer permits it, or when something outside your control forces you to stop — a photo is neither. Hazard lights and a short stop do not create an exception; they just make an illegal, dangerous stop more visible.

questions.prompt: You are driving on a freeway and want to signal that you are moving into the left lane. May you use a hand signal?
options: No — hand signals are prohibited on a freeway
Yes, provided you make the signal clearly and early
Yes, as long as you use your indicators at the same time
questions.explanation: Reg 323(2)(d) prohibits giving a hand signal while driving a motor vehicle on a freeway, so neither a clear early signal nor a left-only one makes it lawful — you use your indicators. At freeway speeds an arm out of the window is both hard to see and a real risk to the driver making it. The prohibition has one narrow escape, 'except for a cause beyond his or her control', which is what covers a driver whose indicators fail mid-journey; it is not a general permission.

questions.prompt: Which one of these vehicles may legally be operated on a freeway?
options: A tractor
A motor tricycle
A motorcycle with a 400 cc engine
questions.explanation: A 400 cc motorcycle is well above the 50 cc cut-off in reg 323(1)(c) and is not electrically propelled, so it is not on the prohibited list. A motor tricycle is named outright in reg 323(1)(d). A tractor is named in reg 323(1)(f), but with one narrow carve-out you should know about: reg 323(4)(a) disapplies that prohibition for a person operating a tractor in connection with the construction or maintenance of a freeway. That is roadworks, not ordinary driving.

questions.prompt: Your indicators have failed and you need to show that you are turning left. Which hand signal do you give?
options: Right arm out of the window with the forearm bent down, circling anti-clockwise
Right arm straight out of the window, level with the shoulder, palm facing forward
Right arm out of the window with the forearm bent up, palm facing forward
questions.explanation: In a car all three prescribed signals are given with the right arm, so the shape of the arm carries the meaning: right arm out with the forearm hanging down and circling anti-clockwise means left (reg 324). The right arm out with the forearm up and the palm facing forward is the signal for stopping or reducing speed suddenly (reg 327), not a turn. The left-arm signal is a real signal — but reg 324's proviso reserves it for the driver of a tractor, a two-wheel vehicle or an animal-drawn vehicle, so it is not available to you in a car.

questions.prompt: The driver in front of you puts their right arm out of the window with the forearm bent upwards and the palm facing forward. What are they telling you?
options: They are about to turn right
They are about to turn left
They are slowing down or about to stop
questions.explanation: Forearm bent up with the palm forward is the signal for slowing or stopping, so you should increase your following distance and be ready to brake. A right turn is signalled with the arm held straight out level with the shoulder, and a left turn with the forearm bent down and circling anti-clockwise.

questions.prompt: An ambulance comes up behind you sounding its siren and showing its emergency identification lamp. What must you do?
options: Hold your position, because a vehicle already on the road keeps its right of way
Give it immediate and absolute right of way, moving to the left as soon as you safely can
Speed up and stay ahead of it until you reach a turnoff where you can leave the road
questions.explanation: Reg 308(1)(h) makes it an offence to fail to give an immediate and absolute right of way to a vehicle sounding its device or bell or displaying its identification lamp under s 58(3) or s 60 of the Act — so the road must open for it and you move left as soon as you safely can. You never hold your right of way against it. Speeding up to stay ahead holds the emergency vehicle back and risks putting you over the speed limit. Worth knowing: the Act only lets that driver disregard road traffic signs and exceed the general speed limit while the device is being sounded AND the identification lamp is in operation.

questions.prompt: You are driving in the right-hand lane of a two-lane road when a fire engine appears behind you with its siren on. What is the correct way to respond?
options: Work out where it is coming from, indicate, and move to the left as soon as it is safe, stopping and waiting if you have to
Brake hard and stop where you are so that it can decide how to get past you
Keep your speed and lane, because moving over could cause a crash with the traffic on your left
questions.explanation: You must clear the path deliberately: identify where the vehicle is coming from, signal, and move left as soon as it is safe, then carry on once it has passed. Stopping dead in a live lane leaves you blocking the road, and staying put is exactly what the immediate-and-absolute rule forbids.

questions.prompt: You have a green light at an intersection when an ambulance with its siren on approaches from your left, against its red light. What must you do?
options: Carry on through, because a green light gives you right of way over other traffic
Hoot to warn the ambulance that you are the one with right of way
Give way immediately and let it through, even though your light is green
questions.explanation: Emergency drivers are allowed to pass signs and signals that would otherwise hold them back, and your duty to give way is immediate and absolute, so the green light does not protect you here. Driving on or hooting both assume a right of way that a siren cancels.

questions.prompt: You are involved in an accident in which a passenger is injured, and you did not give your details to a traffic officer at the scene. By when must you report the accident at a police station?
options: As soon as you reasonably can, and in any case within 24 hours
Within 48 hours
Within 7 days
questions.explanation: If your details were not given to a traffic officer at the scene, you must report at a police station as soon as you reasonably can and within 24 hours, taking your driving licence and ID number. The 48-hour and 7-day options are simply longer than the law allows and would leave you in breach of your duty.

questions.prompt: After a crash in which someone was hurt, you are shaken and a bystander offers you a drink to calm your nerves. What does the law say?
options: It is allowed once the ambulance has taken the injured person away
