You may not drink alcohol or take a narcotic drug before you have reported the accident and, if an officer asks for it, been medically examined
It is allowed as long as you are not going to drive again that day
questions.explanation: Drinking after an accident is barred until you have reported it and submitted to a medical examination if an officer requires one, because alcohol taken afterwards destroys the evidence of your state at the time of the crash. Neither the ambulance leaving nor your decision not to drive again lifts that duty.

questions.prompt: You are approaching an intersection where you intend to turn left. Where must your vehicle be positioned?
options: As near to the left of the roadway as conditions allow, having signaled before you get there
In the middle of your side of the road, so you have room to swing wide into the side street
Just left of the centre line, so following traffic can pass you on the left
questions.explanation: A left turn is made from as near the left of the roadway as conditions allow, with the signal given before you reach the intersection. Sitting in the middle or near the centre line invites traffic up your left-hand side and is exactly the drifting position examiners penalise.

questions.prompt: You are going to turn right at an intersection on an ordinary two-way road. Where should you position your vehicle before the turn?
options: Hard against the right-hand kerb of the road
In the centre of your lane, turning from wherever the lane happens to be
As near as you can get to just left of the middle of the road
questions.explanation: For a right turn on a two-way road you move as close as conditions allow to just left of the middle of the road, which keeps you on your own half while leaving room for traffic to pass on your left. Hugging the right-hand kerb puts you into oncoming traffic, and simply staying centred in your lane blocks the drivers behind you.

questions.prompt: You are correctly positioned and signaling to turn right, but oncoming traffic is steady. When may you begin the turn?
options: As soon as the first oncoming driver has to slow down for you, because you are already committed
Only when there is a gap big enough for you to complete the turn without obstructing or endangering other traffic
Immediately, provided you keep your indicator on throughout the turn
questions.explanation: You may not start a right turn unless you can finish it without obstructing or endangering anyone, so you wait in position for a real gap. Forcing oncoming drivers to brake and relying on your indicator to excuse the move are both the same mistake: an indicator asks for space, it does not grant it.

questions.prompt: You are travelling on a one-way street and want to turn right at the next intersection. Where must you position your vehicle?
options: As near as you can to the right-hand side of the roadway
Just left of the middle of the roadway, as you would on a two-way road
In whichever lane is emptiest, since a one-way street has no oncoming traffic
questions.explanation: On a one-way street the whole roadway is yours to use in one direction, so a right turn is made from as near the right-hand side as you can get. Taking up the middle position needlessly blocks traffic that could pass on your left, and picking the emptiest lane ignores the positioning rule the examiner is marking.

questions.prompt: You are turning right at an intersection on a two-way road. At what point may you cross into the right-hand half of the road?
options: As soon as you have signalled, so that you are lined up well before the intersection
Only once you are inside the intersection itself, keeping left of any traffic island
Once the vehicle in front of you has cleared the intersection
questions.explanation: You stay on your own half of the road up to the intersection and only cross into the right half inside the intersection, passing left of any traffic island. Cutting across early puts you on the wrong side of the road facing oncoming traffic, and the movement of the car ahead of you has nothing to do with where the right half of the road begins.

questions.prompt: You approach a red octagonal sign with the word STOP. What must you do?
options: Come to a complete stop, then proceed when safe
Slow down and proceed if the way looks clear
Stop only if other vehicles are present
questions.explanation: A stop sign requires a complete stop every time, then proceeding when safe — regardless of whether other traffic is present. Slowing or rolling through is a common error confused with the yield sign.

questions.prompt: A solid red circle with a single white horizontal bar means:
options: One-way traffic ahead
No entry — do not pass this point
No overtaking
questions.explanation: The red circle with a white bar is the no-entry sign; you may not proceed past it. It is distinct from a one-way sign (which shows the permitted direction) and a no-overtaking sign.

questions.prompt: A blue circular sign showing the number 60 in white means:
options: Maximum speed 60 km/h
Recommended speed 60 km/h
Minimum speed 60 km/h — do not drive slower
questions.explanation: A blue command circle sets a minimum speed: you must not drive slower than 60. A red-bordered white circle would set a maximum. Blue means 'you must'; a red border means 'you must not'.

questions.prompt: A white circular sign with a red border and a black '80' means:
options: You may not exceed 80 km/h
You must travel at least 80 km/h
Average speed should be 80 km/h
questions.explanation: A red-bordered white circle with a number sets the maximum speed — you may not exceed 80. Driving slower is allowed. A minimum-speed sign would be blue.

questions.prompt: What shape and border identify a permanent warning sign in South Africa?
options: A yellow diamond
A red-bordered triangle (apex up)
A blue circle
questions.explanation: Permanent warning signs are red-bordered triangles standing on their base. A temporary roadworks warning is the same triangle on a yellow background (regulation 286A) — the background changes, the shape does not. A blue circle is a regulatory command sign.

questions.prompt: A red-bordered triangle showing two children means:
options: A school zone where you must stop
A pedestrian crossing for adults only
Children may be present — reduce speed and stay alert
questions.explanation: The children warning calls for reduced speed and heightened alertness because children may enter the road. It is a warning, not a command to stop, and is not limited to adults.

questions.prompt: A red-bordered triangle showing a car with wavy skid lines warns that:
options: The road may be slippery — reduce speed and avoid harsh inputs
There is loose gravel ahead
The road is closed
questions.explanation: The skid symbol warns of a slippery surface; respond by slowing and avoiding harsh braking or steering. It does not mean loose gravel or a road closure.

questions.prompt: A red-bordered triangle with three arrows forming a circle tells you that:
options: You must drive in a circle
A traffic circle is ahead — slow down and be ready to yield
No U-turns are allowed
questions.explanation: W201 warns that a mini-circle or roundabout is ahead. It is a warning, not the yield rule itself — what you must do is set by the sign at the circle. At a roundabout (R137) you yield to traffic already in the circle approaching from your right; at a mini-circle (R2.2) you yield to whoever reaches the yield line first. The sign is not an instruction to drive in circles, nor a U-turn prohibition.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a 'no stopping' sign and a 'no parking' sign?
options: They mean the same thing
Under 'no stopping' you may park but not load
Under 'no parking' you may stop briefly to load; under 'no stopping' you may not stop at all
questions.explanation: No parking permits a brief stop to load or set down passengers; no stopping forbids stopping entirely except in an emergency. They are not the same, and no stopping never permits parking.

questions.prompt: A traffic light is showing a flashing red signal. What must you do?
options: Treat it like a stop sign — stop, then proceed when safe
Drive through, as the signal is faulty
Speed up to clear the intersection
questions.explanation: A flashing red signal is treated like a stop sign: stop fully, then proceed when safe. It is not a malfunction to ignore, and speeding through is dangerous and unlawful.

questions.prompt: A steady amber (yellow) traffic light means:
options: Speed up to beat the red
Prepare to stop; stop if you can do so safely
Proceed with right of way over all traffic
questions.explanation: Amber means prepare to stop and stop if it is safe to do so — not accelerate to beat the red. It is the single most-misunderstood signal.

questions.prompt: A single solid white line running along the centre of the road on your side means:
options: You may cross it to overtake when safe
It only marks the road edge
It is a barrier line — do not cross or straddle it
questions.explanation: A solid line on your side is a no-crossing barrier line. A broken line, by contrast, may be crossed when safe. It is not merely an edge marker.

questions.prompt: A red-bordered triangle showing a walking person means:
options: A pedestrian crossing is ahead — be ready to stop
This is a pedestrian crossing — you must stop
Pedestrians are prohibited
questions.explanation: The triangular sign warns that a pedestrian crossing is ahead; slow and be ready to stop. The blue rectangular sign marks the crossing itself. It does not prohibit pedestrians.

questions.prompt: You are warned of a railway level crossing ahead. What must you never do?
options: Look both ways before crossing
Stop or queue with your vehicle on the tracks
Slow down on the approach
questions.explanation: You must never stop or queue on the railway tracks. Looking both ways and slowing down are correct behaviours on the approach.

questions.prompt: A blue circle with an arrow angling left around an obstruction means:
options: Turn left at the next intersection
Left lane closed
Pass to the left of the island or obstruction
questions.explanation: The keep-left command directs you to pass to the left of the marked island or obstruction. It is a positioning instruction, not a turn instruction or a lane closure.

questions.prompt: A red rectangular sign with a single white arrow indicates:
options: Traffic flows in the arrow's direction only
No entry for heavy vehicles
A dead-end road
questions.explanation: The one-way roadway sign (R4) shows the single permitted direction of travel; no opposing traffic should be expected. It is not a heavy-vehicle restriction or a dead-end marker. Do not confuse its red background with the blue keep-left sign R103, which routes you around an obstacle.

questions.prompt: What does a large green sign with white place names, arrows and yellow route numbers tell you?
options: You must turn at the next exit
It gives directions to routes and destinations ahead
It is a speed-limit sign
questions.explanation: A green direction sign is a guidance sign giving routes and destinations ahead of a junction. It carries no command, and it is not a speed-limit sign.

questions.prompt: What is the background colour of a sign directing you to a tourist attraction?
options: Red
Green
Brown
questions.explanation: Tourism signs use a brown background with white text. Red borders denote prohibition, and green denotes freeway/rural direction — neither is used for tourism.

questions.prompt: What shape is an information sign in South Africa?
options: Rectangular
Triangular
Circular
questions.explanation: Information signs are rectangular. Shape is the quickest way to tell the classes apart: a circle is regulatory and a triangle is a warning.

questions.prompt: You see a rectangular sign showing the letter 'P'. What does it indicate?
options: You must stop and park here
Parking is available here
No parking is allowed
questions.explanation: The blue rectangular 'P' (R305-P) marks an area reserved for parking — it tells you parking is available, not that you must park there. The round 'P' in a red ring (R216) is the opposite: it prohibits parking.

questions.prompt: A sign showing the letter 'H' means:
options: Heavy vehicles only
A hazard ahead
A hospital / emergency medical services are ahead
questions.explanation: The 'H' service symbol indicates a hospital or emergency medical services ahead. It is informational, not a heavy-vehicle restriction or a hazard warning.

questions.prompt: On a freeway you pass rectangular signs showing three bars, then two, then one. What do they mean?
options: A countdown of the distance to the next exit (300 m, 200 m, 100 m)
The number of lanes ahead
A speed reducing in steps
questions.explanation: Countdown markers show three, two and one diagonal bars at 300, 200 and 100 metres before a freeway exit, so you can prepare to leave at speed. They are not lane counts or a stepped speed limit.

questions.prompt: A red-bordered triangle showing an inverted T means:
options: A pedestrian crossing ahead
The road ends ahead — you must turn left or right
A T-shaped building ahead
questions.explanation: The inverted-T warning means your road terminates at a T-junction and you must turn. It is not a pedestrian or building sign, and you cannot continue straight.

questions.prompt: A triangle showing two vertical arrows, one up and one down, warns that:
options: It is a one-way road ahead
You must keep left
The road becomes two-way — expect oncoming traffic
questions.explanation: Opposed up/down arrows warn that a one-way section becomes two-way, so expect oncoming traffic. It is not a one-way or keep-left sign.

questions.prompt: A triangle with edges angling inward warns that:
options: The road narrows ahead
The road ends ahead
Lanes merge into a one-way street
questions.explanation: Inward-angling edges warn the carriageway narrows ahead; slow and adjust position. It does not mean the road ends or becomes one-way.

questions.prompt: You see a warning sign for a steep descent. What is the safest action?
options: Coast in neutral to save fuel
Select a lower gear before descending
Keep the clutch pressed down the hill
questions.explanation: On a steep descent select a lower gear so engine braking helps control speed and saves the brakes. Coasting in neutral or riding the clutch removes engine braking and is dangerous.

questions.prompt: Which sign shows a car with curved skid marks behind its wheels?
options: The gravel-road-begins sign
The loose-stones sign
The slippery-road sign
questions.explanation: The skidding-car symbol is the slippery-road sign. The gravel-begins sign shows tar ending and gravel starting; loose-stones shows a wheel throwing up stones. The test exploits this three-way confusion.

questions.prompt: A triangle showing a raised rounded-mound profile warns of:
options: Speed humps ahead
An uneven, potholed road
A narrow bridge
questions.explanation: The rounded-mound profile warns of speed humps; slow enough to cross safely. The jagged profile is uneven roadway, and a bridge sign shows pinching parapets.

questions.prompt: A triangle showing a leaping buck warns of:
options: Domestic cattle on the road
Wild animals (game) that may cross
A hunting area where you must stop
questions.explanation: The leaping-buck symbol warns of wild game crossing. A cattle silhouette would be the domestic-animals sign. It is a warning, not a command to stop.

questions.prompt: A round white sign with a red ring and a left arrow crossed by a red slash means:
options: You must turn left
Left lane for buses only
You may not turn left
questions.explanation: A red ring and slash make it a prohibition: you may not turn left. A blue circle with a white left arrow would command the turn instead. Colour signals the meaning.

questions.prompt: A round prohibition sign with two vertical arrows pointing toward each other and '4,4 m' means:
options: Vehicles taller than 4.4 m may not pass
Vehicles wider than 4.4 m may not pass
Minimum height 4.4 m to pass
questions.explanation: Vertical arrows indicate a height limit — vehicles taller than 4.4 m are prohibited. Horizontal arrows would indicate a width limit. It is a maximum, not a minimum.

questions.prompt: A round prohibition sign with two horizontal arrows pointing toward each other and a measurement means:
options: A height limit
A width limit — wider vehicles prohibited
A following-distance instruction
questions.explanation: Horizontal arrows indicate a width limit; vehicles wider than the stated measurement are prohibited. Vertical arrows would be a height limit.

questions.prompt: A round white sign with a red ring and a truck symbol means:
options: All vehicles are prohibited
A truck stop is ahead
Goods/heavy vehicles are prohibited
questions.explanation: The red-ringed truck sign prohibits goods vehicles. Note that regulation 1 defines a goods vehicle by what it is built to carry, not by its size — a bakkie is a goods vehicle, so this sign is not limited to large trucks. It does not ban all traffic, nor does it indicate a truck stop.

questions.prompt: A blue circle with three white arrows forming a clockwise loop tells you to:
options: Yield to traffic in the circle and proceed clockwise
Make a U-turn
Stop completely before entering
questions.explanation: The blue roundabout command directs you to circulate clockwise, yielding to traffic already in the circle and from your right. It is not a U-turn or an automatic full-stop sign.

questions.prompt: A blue circle with a white arrow curving left means:
options: You may not turn left
You must turn left ahead
Left lane closed
questions.explanation: A blue circle is a command: you must turn left. The red-ringed version would prohibit the turn. Blue means 'you must'; a red border means 'you must not'.

questions.prompt: At roadworks you pass a sign carrying the usual warning symbol, but on a yellow background inside a red triangle. What is the yellow telling you?
options: The sign is temporary, and it overrides a permanent sign that says otherwise
The sign is only advisory, so the permanent signs still decide
The sign applies to heavy vehicles only
questions.explanation: Yellow marks the sign as temporary, and a temporary sign wins where it conflicts with a permanent one — the bolted-down sign does not outrank it. Temporary signs are not only for roadworks: accident scenes and signals out of order use them too.

questions.prompt: At roadworks a worker holds a board showing a red STOP face toward you. What must you do?
options: Stop and wait until the GO face is shown
Proceed slowly past the worker
Sound your hooter and continue
questions.explanation: A Stop/Go board controls a single open lane through the works — on the red STOP face you must stop and wait until the green GO face is shown. Proceeding risks a head-on collision in the works zone.

questions.prompt: A broken white line is painted along the centre of the road on your side. What does it allow?
options: You may never cross it
You may cross it to overtake when it is safe
It marks a no-stopping zone
questions.explanation: A broken line may be crossed to overtake or change lanes when it is safe. A solid line on your side is the no-crossing barrier. It is not a no-stopping marking.

questions.prompt: A broken white line is painted across your lane at a junction. What does it mean?
options: Stop completely behind the line
Yield — give way, stopping only if necessary
A pedestrian crossing is ahead
questions.explanation: A broken white line across your lane is a yield line (RTM2): give way at that point, stopping only if you must. A solid line across the lane is a stop line (RTM1) and requires a complete stop. Two solid lines with a gap between them mark a pedestrian crossing (RTM3).

questions.prompt: A round white sign with a red ring and a U-shaped arrow crossed by a red slash means:
options: You may not make a U-turn here
You must make a U-turn
No right turn
questions.explanation: The red-slashed U-arrow prohibits a U-turn at this point. It does not command a U-turn, and it is distinct from a no-right-turn sign.

questions.prompt: A triangular sign with a red border, showing a pedestrian on zebra stripes, means:
options: Pedestrians are prohibited on this stretch of road
You are at the crossing now — give way to anyone already on it
A marked pedestrian crossing is ahead
questions.explanation: A red triangle warns of something ahead — the crossing is still in front of you, so slow down and be ready to stop. The crossing itself carries no sign panel; it is the painted lines on the road. Give way to anyone already on it when you get there.

questions.prompt: At a railway crossing the boom is down and the red lights are flashing. What must you do?
options: Drive around the boom if no train is visible
Sound your hooter and cross quickly
Stop and wait until the boom lifts and the lights stop
questions.explanation: You must stop and wait until the boom lifts and the lights stop — a train is approaching. Driving around a boom is extremely dangerous and unlawful.

questions.prompt: A solid white line is painted across your lane at a stop street. Where must the vehicle come to a standstill?
options: Immediately behind the line
With the front wheels resting on the line
Level with the Stop sign, wherever the line happens to be
questions.explanation: A stop line tells you exactly where to stop: the vehicle must come to a complete standstill immediately behind it, not on it and not beyond it. The line is often set back from the sign so you can see across the junction, so stopping level with the sign puts you too far forward.

questions.prompt: You arrive at a junction where a stop line is painted across your lane, but the Stop sign has been knocked down. What must you do?
options: Stop as though the Stop sign were still standing
Treat it as a yield and drive on if the way is clear
Ignore the line, because a marking has no force without its sign
questions.explanation: At a junction, where the Stop sign has fallen down or the signal is out of order, the stop line carries the full force of the Stop sign on its own. A missing sign does not downgrade the line to a yield, and it certainly does not cancel it.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a yield line painted across your lane is correct?
options: It carries the significance of a Yield sign, even where that sign is missing
It only applies while a Yield sign is standing beside it
It requires you to stop completely, like a stop line
questions.explanation: A yield line carries the significance of Yield sign R2, including where that sign has fallen down. Yielding is not stopping — you may keep moving if the way is genuinely clear — but the duty to give way does not depend on the sign still being there.

questions.prompt: A vehicle ahead of you has stopped at a pedestrian crossing to let someone cross. What may you do?
options: Nothing — you may not pass a vehicle stopped at a pedestrian crossing
Pass it on the right, slowly, if you can see the crossing is clear on your side
Pass it on the left, since the pedestrian is on the other side of the road
questions.explanation: Where a vehicle has stopped at a pedestrian crossing to let people cross, a driver coming up behind may not pass it. The stopped vehicle is hiding the crossing from you and from the pedestrian, which is exactly when someone steps out.

questions.prompt: A pedestrian crossing is marked by two solid white lines with a gap between them. Where does the driver actually stop?
options: At the stop line or yield line painted before the crossing
On the crossing itself, level with the first white line
Anywhere within the gap between the two lines
questions.explanation: The crossing is preceded by a stop line or a yield line, and that is where the driver stops — the corridor between the two white lines is the pedestrians' space, not a place to bring a vehicle to rest.

questions.prompt: A row of wide white blocks is painted across the road outside a school. What are they?
options: A pedestrian crossing, where people crossing have right of way
Speed bumps, which you must slow down for
A no-stopping zone, which you may drive across but not stop on
questions.explanation: The blocks are a high-visibility pedestrian crossing, laid out so it can be seen from a distance. They are flat paint, not speed bumps, and the duty they carry is to give way to a pedestrian crossing — not merely to slow down.

questions.prompt: A block pedestrian crossing also has a traffic signal at it. Which controls you?
options: The signal — an accompanying sign or signal takes precedence over the marking
The marking — paint on the road always outranks a signal
Whichever you reach first
questions.explanation: Where a crossing is used together with a road sign, a traffic signal, a stop line or a yield line, that control takes precedence over the marking itself. The blocks tell you a crossing is there; the signal tells you when to go.

questions.prompt: A single solid white line runs down the middle of a two-way road. In which of these situations may you cross it?
options: To pass a stationary obstruction in the road, when it is safe
To overtake a slow vehicle, if the road ahead is clear
Never — a solid line may not be crossed for any reason
questions.explanation: You may cross it to get past a stationary obstruction in the road, and only when it is safe. Overtaking is the one thing the line exists to prevent, and 'never for any reason' is also wrong — access to property and a stationary obstruction are both allowed for.

questions.prompt: What is the practical difference between a single solid white line and two solid white lines down the middle of the road?
options: The single line still lets you turn across it into a property; the double lines do not
There is none — both simply mean no overtaking
The double lines may be crossed at any time if the road is clear
questions.explanation: Both bar overtaking, but the single line still permits you to turn across it to enter or leave property. Two lines are stricter: the only reason to cross them is a stationary obstruction in the roadway, so the turn into a driveway is out.

questions.prompt: You are behind double solid white lines and a broken-down truck is partly blocking your lane. What may you do?
options: Cross the lines to pass it, when it is safe to do so
Wait behind it until it is moved, because the lines may never be crossed
Drive on the shoulder to get around it
questions.explanation: A stationary obstruction in the roadway is the one reason you may cross double white lines, and only when it is safe. The obstruction does not have to be blocking the road completely. Using the shoulder is not an alternative — passing on the shoulder is prohibited.

questions.prompt: What does the solid yellow line along the left edge of the roadway mark?
options: The edge of the roadway, with the shoulder beyond it
A lane reserved for slow-moving vehicles
A no-parking zone
questions.explanation: The yellow edge line marks where the roadway ends. The strip beyond it, between the line and the kerb, is the shoulder — and the shoulder is not a normal traffic lane, not a slow lane for you to sit in.

questions.prompt: On a road with one lane in each direction, when may you move onto the shoulder to let a faster vehicle pass?
options: Between sunrise and sunset, if you endanger nobody and people and vehicles are visible at least 150 m away
At any time, as long as you indicate first
Only at night, when you can see the other vehicle's headlights
questions.explanation: The courtesy move is a narrow daytime exception: between sunrise and sunset, on a road with one lane each direction, only while you are actually being overtaken, only if you endanger nobody, and only where people and vehicles are clearly discernible at least 150 metres away. At night it is not available at all.

questions.prompt: A painted island is marked off in the middle of the road. What may you do with it?
options: Nothing — you may not drive on it, stop on it or park on it
Drive across it, as long as you do not stop on it
Use it to wait for a gap when you are turning right
questions.explanation: A painted island is out of bounds for all three: driving on it, stopping on it and parking on it. Using it as a waiting space to turn is the common error, and because no part of the vehicle may enter it, a single wheel is enough.

questions.prompt: How do you recognise a painted island?
options: By the boundary lines enclosing it — the area inside usually carries yellow bars, but not always
By the yellow diagonal bars, which every painted island has
By its red border, which no other marking uses
questions.explanation: The boundary is what defines it. The area inside is normally filled with yellow sloping bars in a diagonal or chevron pattern, but one form has no bars at all — two solid white lines enclosing a plain yellow area. A learner who looks only for stripes will not recognise that one.

questions.prompt: How must a vehicle be positioned in a marked parking bay?
options: Wholly within the lines defining the bay
With at least three wheels inside the bay
Roughly central, with a little overhang allowed at either end
questions.explanation: The requirement is that the vehicle is parked wholly within the lines defining the limits of the bay. A wheel over the line means it is no longer wholly within, and 'roughly central' is not the test.

questions.prompt: A parking bay is outlined in yellow with the letter T in a yellow oval. What does that mean?
options: Only a taxi may park or stop there
Any vehicle may park there for a limited time
It is a temporary bay, in use only while roadworks are underway
questions.explanation: A yellow bay with a lettered oval is reserved for the class the letter indicates — T for taxi — and the prohibition covers stopping as well as parking. The letter is not a time limit and not a temporary marking.

questions.prompt: Which vehicle may stop in a bay marked with the letter L?
options: A goods vehicle, or a motorcycle or tricycle designed to carry goods
Any vehicle, as long as the driver is loading something
Only a truck above 3 500 kg
questions.explanation: An L bay is a loading zone, and it admits a goods vehicle as well as a motorcycle, motor tricycle or motor quadrucycle designed or adapted to convey goods — four categories, not one. Having something to carry does not make an ordinary car eligible.

questions.prompt: Your lane is marked with a yellow arrow pointing left and a second pointing straight ahead. What may you do from that lane?
options: Either turn left or go straight ahead, but nothing else
Only turn left, because the left arrow comes first
Anything, because the arrows are advisory
questions.explanation: Where two directions are shown, either one is permitted and nothing else is. The arrows are mandatory, not advisory — three of the six variants show one direction and three show a choice of two.

questions.prompt: A broken yellow line runs along the side of a lane with the word BUS painted in it. May you drive in that lane?
options: No — it is reserved, and the broken line is not an invitation to use it
Yes, because a broken line always means you may cross into the lane
Yes, provided you leave the lane before the next junction
questions.explanation: The lane is reserved for the class of vehicle shown, and the gaps in the yellow line are just how the boundary is drawn — not permission, the way a broken white lane line would be. The reservation is granted by the accompanying sign, not by the paint.

questions.prompt: You are going straight ahead and the yellow box junction in front of you is clear, but the traffic beyond it is standing still. What must you do?
options: Wait behind the box until you can expect to clear it
Move into the box and wait there for the traffic to move
Enter the box, because it is clear at the moment you arrive
questions.explanation: The rule bites at the moment you enter: do not enter if stationary vehicles ahead mean you will not be able to leave. An empty box is not the test — where you will be able to get to is.

questions.prompt: Which vehicles may enter a yellow box junction even when the exit is not clear?
options: Vehicles turning left or right
None — the box may never be entered unless the exit is clear
Emergency vehicles only
questions.explanation: A vehicle turning left or turning right may enter the box. That is an exception written into the rule, and it is the part learners most often miss because the box looks like a blanket prohibition.

questions.prompt: What does a solid red line along the edge of the road mean?
options: No stopping at all, 24 hours a day
No parking, but a brief stop to drop someone off is allowed
No stopping, but only during the hours shown on a nearby sign
questions.explanation: A solid red line bans stopping around the clock. Stopping is much wider than parking, so a quick drop-off is out. A broken red line is the one that applies only during the hours shown on the accompanying sign.

questions.prompt: You pull up next to a solid yellow line and sit in the car with the engine running, waiting for a passenger to come out. Is that allowed?
options: No — waiting for someone is parking, not loading
Yes, because you never left the vehicle
Yes, as long as you stay less than five minutes
questions.explanation: Parking in law means keeping a vehicle, whether occupied or not, stationary for longer than is reasonably necessary to load or unload people or goods. Sitting in the driver's seat changes nothing, and there is no five-minute allowance — the test is whether you are actually loading.

questions.prompt: Yellow arrows are painted around the circle at a mini circle. Which way must you travel?
options: Clockwise, keeping the circle on your right
Anti-clockwise, keeping the circle on your left
Whichever way is shorter to your exit
questions.explanation: The arrows impose a mandatory direction: you travel clockwise, so the circle stays on your right. Cutting across in front of it to shorten a right turn breaks that direction, whatever the traffic is doing.

questions.prompt: You are approaching a T-junction. A green sign shows the road layout with the whole bar across the top of the 'T' coloured red. What is it telling you?
options: Only the right-hand arm of the crossing road is a dead end.
The road crossing your path is a dead end - there is no way through in either direction.
The crossing road is one-way and you may not turn into it.
questions.explanation: The red bar sits on the road that crosses your path, so neither way along it goes through. If your destination is not on that short street, don't turn in - you will have to turn around and come back out.

questions.prompt: The road ahead branches. A green dead-end sign shows the branch layout with the right-hand arm coloured red. What does the red arm tell you?
options: The right-hand branch is a no-through road; the other branch carries on.
The left-hand branch is the no-through road.
You are not allowed to turn right here.
questions.explanation: The red arm is the one that is closed. Here it is the right-hand branch, so turning right ends in a cul-de-sac. Keep to the through route unless the address you want is actually on that branch.

questions.prompt: You are looking for a friend's street, which is the left-hand one where the road ahead splits. The green dead-end sign shows the left arm in red. What should you expect if you take it?
options: The right-hand branch is the dead end, so the left one carries on through.
The left-hand branch is closed to traffic and you may not enter it.
The left-hand branch has no exit at the far end - you would have to come back out the same way.
questions.explanation: The red arm shows which branch is closed, and on this sign it is the left one. It is not a banned turn: you may drive in, but there is no way out at the far end, so you return the way you came.

questions.prompt: A yellow diamond priority-road sign tells you that you are on a priority road. What does that actually give you?
options: Traffic entering from the side roads you pass must give way to you.
Right of way over everything ahead, including at traffic signals.
You must give way to traffic coming out of the side roads.
questions.explanation: The priority-road sign settles one thing only: who gives way at the side roads you pass. They yield to you. It changes nothing at traffic signals, stop signs or pedestrian crossings, so keep watching.

questions.prompt: A green information sign carries a single white letter 'i'. What is ahead?
options: A police station.
A hospital or first-aid post.
A travel information centre.
questions.explanation: The white 'i' is the information symbol - maps, directions and local advice. A hospital is shown by an 'H'. Nothing is required of you here; stop only if you actually want travel information.

questions.prompt: A green sign shows a traffic-light symbol next to the number 60. What does the 60 mean?
options: The speed limit drops to 60 until the last set of lights.
The lights ahead are timed so that holding about 60 keeps you moving through on green.
You may not drive slower than 60 until the last set of lights.
questions.explanation: The number is the speed the lights are timed for - not a limit and not a minimum. Hold a steady speed near it, within the legal limit, and you should ride the greens. You still stop for any red.

questions.prompt: You are approaching a traffic light and a green sign next to it reads '3 PHASE'. What should you expect?
options: Three separate sets of traffic lights follow one after the other.
The signal runs in three separate stages, so your green may only come later in the cycle.
All directions share the same green, so you may move as soon as any light turns green.
questions.explanation: Multi-phase means the cycle is split into stages, each releasing different movements. A green somewhere in the intersection is not your green - wait for the signal facing your lane and be patient.

questions.prompt: An information sign showing a bus symbol appears at the side of the road. What is it telling you?
options: There is a bus stop ahead - expect buses stopping and passengers near the road.
The lane ahead is reserved for buses and you may not drive in it.
You must give way to every bus from this point onwards.
questions.explanation: The bus symbol here is information, not a command: it marks a stop ahead. Expect a bus to pull in or pull away, and passengers stepping out near the road, so leave room and cover the brake.

questions.prompt: An information sign indicates a modal transfer point ahead. What is there?
options: A weighbridge where heavy vehicles are weighed.
A place where travellers change between transport modes, such as bus, taxi and train.
The point where the freeway ends and an ordinary road begins.
questions.explanation: A modal transfer point is where people swap between bus, taxi and train. The hazard is people: passengers crossing to reach it and vehicles stopping to drop them off, so ease off and look early.

questions.prompt: A stop sign has a panel below it showing an arrow curving left. Who has to come to a complete standstill?
options: Nobody — the arrow downgrades the whole sign to a give-way
Everyone except drivers turning left, who only have to give way
Only drivers turning left; everyone else may carry on if the way is clear
questions.explanation: The arrow panel carves out one movement only: drivers turning left give way instead of stopping. Everyone going straight or turning right still comes to a complete standstill at the line.

questions.prompt: A stop sign carries a panel reading '4'. What is it telling you about the intersection?
options: Every one of the four approaches has a stop sign
You are the fourth vehicle in the queue
Four vehicles may cross at a time
questions.explanation: The number counts the approaches that are stop-controlled, not vehicles. At a four-way stop every driver must come to a complete standstill — nobody has an automatic right to go first because their road looks bigger.

questions.prompt: A stop sign has the number 3 on a small panel with it. What does the number tell you?
options: You must stand still for three seconds before pulling off
Three approaches to this intersection each have a stop sign
Three roads join ahead, but only your road has to stop
questions.explanation: The number counts how many approaches are stop-controlled — here, three. Every one of them must stop, so arriving on what looks like the main road gives you nothing.

questions.prompt: A downward-pointing yield triangle has a panel showing a walking person. What must you do?
options: Give way to crossing vehicles; people on foot wait for you
Nothing yet — it warns that pedestrians may be about further on
Give way to people on foot, stopping if you need to before you go on
questions.explanation: The walking-person panel changes who you are yielding to. This is not a warning that people might be about — it is an instruction to let them go first, stopping if you must before you move off.

questions.prompt: You approach a mini circle with a yield triangle showing a circle of arrows. Which vehicle must you give way to?
options: Only vehicles already driving round the circle
Only vehicles approaching from your right
Any vehicle that will reach the yield line before you and cross your path
questions.explanation: It is the yield line that settles it, not whether a car is already going round. If another vehicle gets there first and its path crosses yours, it goes first. Move clockwise and try not to drive over the circle itself.

questions.prompt: A red rectangular sign shows a white arrow pointing to the right. Does it order you to turn right?
options: Yes — you must turn right here
No — it warns that the road bends sharply right ahead
No — it tells you the roadway runs one way, to the right
questions.explanation: A red one-way sign describes the road, it does not order a turn. The arrow shows the direction traffic on that roadway runs — you may travel that way, and you may never drive against it.

questions.prompt: A red diamond-shaped sign shows a walking person, marking a pedestrian precinct. Which vehicles may go in?
options: Any vehicle, as long as it gives way to people on foot
Only vehicles delivering or loading goods, doing maintenance, or emergency vehicles
No vehicle at all, under any circumstances
questions.explanation: Most drivers may not enter at all — the precinct is open only to deliveries, maintenance and emergency vehicles. If you are one of those, you give way to every pedestrian in or about to cross your path, and keep to 15 km/h.

questions.prompt: A sign in a red ring shows two arrows: a red one pointing up and a black one pointing down towards you. Who goes first through the narrow section?
options: You do — oncoming traffic must wait for you
Neither — both directions share the space and squeeze past
Oncoming traffic does — you wait for it to come through
questions.explanation: Red marks the direction that must give way, and that is yours — the red arrow runs away from you up the sign. The black arrow is the traffic coming towards you, and it has the road. Hold back and let it clear the narrow bit.

questions.prompt: You reach a junction where a blue circle shows a straight white arrow pointing right. May you carry straight on?
options: Yes — the arrow only suggests the easiest route through the junction.
No — right is the only direction you may take here.
Yes, as long as you first give way to traffic coming from the right.
questions.explanation: Blue circle means you must. A straight arrow pointing right makes right the only way you may go — no straight on, no left, no U-turn. It is an instruction, not a suggestion.

questions.prompt: A blue circle with a white arrow pointing straight up stands at a junction that has an open side road on your left. What may you do?
options: Go straight ahead only — you may not turn into the side road.
Go straight ahead, or turn left into the side road if it is safe.
Go straight ahead, but only after stopping at the junction first.
questions.explanation: The blue circle commands the one movement it shows. It does not merely allow you to go straight — it forbids turning, so the side road is out even when it is clear and looks inviting.

questions.prompt: A blue circle showing a walking person marks the way ahead. What must a driver do?
options: Drive on with care — people on foot are kept out of that area.
Drive on, but expect a pedestrian crossing a little further ahead.
Not drive in at all — the way ahead is set aside for people on foot.
questions.explanation: A blue circle reserves the space for whoever is pictured, so this route belongs to people on foot and vehicles stay out. The same figure inside a red ring would mean the opposite: no pedestrians.

questions.prompt: The lane beside you is marked with a blue circle containing a bicycle. What does that mean for you as a driver?
options: The lane is shared, so you may use it as long as you watch for cyclists.
The lane is reserved for pedal cyclists, so keep your vehicle out of it.
Cyclists are kept out of that lane, so you may use it freely.
questions.explanation: A bicycle on blue reserves the lane for pedal cycles, so motor vehicles stay out even when it looks empty. It is not an invitation to share, and it is not the sign that keeps bicycles away.

questions.prompt: A path is marked with a blue circle showing a bicycle and a walking person with a line down the middle between them. What does that line tell you?
options: Only the half nearest the road is open; the other half is closed.
Cyclists and pedestrians may mix freely anywhere along the path.
Cyclists and pedestrians each keep to their own side of the path.
questions.explanation: Without a divider the two share the whole width and must look out for each other. The line splits the path instead: bicycles stay on the bicycle side, people on foot on the walker side.

questions.prompt: You are driving a car and the road ahead is marked with a blue circle showing a motorcycle. What must you do?
options: Take another route — that road is set aside for motorcycles.
Carry on, but give way to any motorcycle that comes past you.
Carry on — the sign is there to warn you that motorcycles use the road.
questions.explanation: The blue circle names who the road is for, and here that is motorcycles alone. Cars, bakkies and trucks must keep out. It is not a warning that motorbikes may be about.

questions.prompt: A blue circle shows a car with a sign on its roof. Which vehicles may use that lane?
options: Any motor car.
Any vehicle that is carrying passengers.
Taxis only.
questions.explanation: The roof sign is the detail that decides it. A plain car on blue would reserve the lane for motor cars in general; the car with a roof sign narrows it to taxis, so ordinary cars stay out.

questions.prompt: The lane ahead is marked with a blue circle showing a minibus. How binding is that sign on other drivers?
options: It is only advice — you may use the lane if you are not delaying anyone.
It is compulsory — only minibuses may use that lane.
It is compulsory during peak hours and advice at other times.
questions.explanation: Blue circles are commands and bind you just as tightly as a red prohibition does. A minibus on blue keeps the lane for minibuses, so driving a car in it is an offence at any hour.

questions.prompt: A lane is reserved by a blue circle showing a full-size bus. You are driving a minibus. May you use that lane?
options: Yes — a minibus counts as a bus for this sign.
Yes, provided you are carrying passengers at the time.
No — that lane is for full-size buses, and minibuses have their own sign.
questions.explanation: The picture sets the exact class allowed. A full-size bus means buses; minibuses and midibuses each have a sign of their own, so a minibus belongs in the general traffic lanes.

questions.prompt: A blue circle shows a goods vehicle with the figure '10 t' on it. What does that weight mean?
options: Goods vehicles heavier than 10 t are kept out of this lane.
Only goods vehicles heavier than 10 t may use this lane.
Any vehicle may use the lane as long as it stays under 10 t.
questions.explanation: On a blue command circle the figure is the weight a goods vehicle must be over before it may use the lane, not a limit it has to stay under. A weight ban comes on a white sign with a red ring.

questions.prompt: A blue circle carries the orange diamond used to mark dangerous goods. What is it telling you?
options: Vehicles carrying dangerous goods are kept off this route.
There is a depot storing dangerous goods further ahead.
The route is set aside for vehicles carrying dangerous goods.
questions.explanation: The orange diamond identifies dangerous goods and the blue circle reserves the road for them. This is the route those loads must take, not one they are being kept away from.

questions.prompt: You see a tractor inside a blue circle at the entrance to a side road. What does it mean?
options: Slow farm vehicles may be using the road ahead of you.
The road is reserved for farm vehicles, so other traffic keeps out.
Tractors are not allowed to turn into that road.
questions.explanation: The shape tells you the job of the sign. A warning about tractors would arrive as a red-bordered triangle; a tractor on a blue circle instead sets that road aside for agricultural vehicles.

questions.prompt: A blue circle showing the letter 'T' stands beside the road. What must the driver do?
options: Give way at the T-junction coming up.
Follow the tourist route that starts here.
Pay the toll ahead.
questions.explanation: Here the T stands for toll, and a blue circle is an instruction you must obey: carry on to the plaza, stop if required and pay before going further. It has nothing to do with a T-junction.

questions.prompt: A blue circle showing a lamp shining a beam appears just before a tunnel. What must you switch on?
options: Your hazard lights.
Your headlamps.
Your parking lights.
questions.explanation: Parking lights and daytime running lights are not enough — the sign calls for full headlamps, and they stay on for the whole stretch it covers, usually a tunnel or a section with poor visibility.

questions.prompt: You are driving a bakkie loaded with building sand and you come up behind a slow truck. A red-ringed sign shows two trucks side by side. May you overtake the truck?
options: Yes — the sign is for big rigs, and a bakkie is a light vehicle
No — a bakkie is built to carry goods, so the sign covers you too
Yes, as long as you can pass without crossing a barrier line
questions.explanation: "Goods vehicle" is about what the vehicle is built to carry, not how big it is — so a bakkie counts. This sign stops goods vehicles passing goods vehicles. Stay behind the truck.

questions.prompt: A round white sign with a red ring shows a person walking. What is it telling you?
options: Watch out for people crossing the road ahead
People on foot may not go beyond this sign
There is a pedestrian crossing ahead where you must give way
questions.explanation: The red ring is a prohibition and the figure says who it is aimed at: people on foot may not go beyond it. It says nothing about how drivers must behave, so it is not a warning that pedestrians are about.

questions.prompt: Just before a hospital you pass a white circle with a red ring showing a hooter with a line through it. How far does the silence apply?
options: For 100 m after the sign
Until the next intersection
For the whole length of the road ahead
questions.explanation: The ban runs for 100 metres past the sign, not indefinitely — that distance is the part worth remembering. The same sign also stops you driving past it in a vehicle making more noise than the law allows.

questions.prompt: You are a short way back from a crossroads when you pass a red-ringed sign showing a right arrow that bends, with a line through it. Where does the ban apply?
options: At the crossroads ahead — you may not turn right there
Right at the sign — you may not turn right into anything you are passing
On the whole road — you may not turn right anywhere along it
questions.explanation: The bend in the arrow puts the ban at the junction ahead, not where you are standing. A straight arrow in the red ring means no right turn right here. Check which arrow it is before you choose your lane.

questions.prompt: A round white sign with a red ring shows "12 t". What is it limiting?
options: Speed — nothing may travel faster than 12 km/h past this point
Mass — a vehicle heavier than 12 tonnes may not go past
Length — a vehicle longer than 12 metres may not go past
questions.explanation: The number is a mass in tonnes. If you are towing, it is the mass of the whole combination that counts, not just the vehicle pulling — so a lighter bakkie with a loaded trailer can still be over the limit.

questions.prompt: You are towing a caravan on holiday and you come to a red-ringed sign showing a trailer. Does it apply to you?
options: No — it stops trucks pulling heavy goods trailers
Yes — any vehicle that is towing another must not go past
No — it applies only to a vehicle being towed away after a breakdown
questions.explanation: The picture is a trailer, but the ban is on towing. A car with a caravan, a bakkie with a light trailer, a tow truck with a broken-down car — all of them have to find another route here.

questions.prompt: You pass a red-ringed sign showing a crossed-out thumbs-up just as someone at the roadside signals for a lift. What does that sign require of you, the driver?
options: Nothing — it is aimed at the hitch-hiker, not at the driver
You may not stop to pick the person up
You may pick them up if you stop well clear of the roadway
questions.explanation: It binds you as well as the hitch-hiker: for 500 m past the sign no driver may pick up passengers and nobody on foot may thumb for a lift. It does not stop you halting for any other reason.

questions.prompt: An island separates a bus lane on the left from the rest of the road. The blue circle facing you on that island carries an arrow angling downwards to the right. What must you do?
options: Stop and give way to any bus using the lane on the left.
Pass the island on its right-hand side and stay out of the bus lane.
Turn right at the next junction — no other direction is allowed.
questions.explanation: The arrow points down at about 45 degrees towards the side you must pass on, so keep right of the island and leave the left lane to the buses. A straight horizontal arrow would be a different order: right only.

questions.prompt: You come round a bend and find temporary signs set up beside the road. What are they telling you?
options: That the road has been permanently changed and these signs will stay there for good
That the road ahead is closed and you must turn around
That conditions on this stretch are not normal right now, so what you would usually expect may not apply
questions.explanation: Temporary signs go up for a temporary condition. The message is simply that things here are not normal today. Drive to what the signs in front of you say, not to what you remember about this road.

questions.prompt: A temporary sign and a permanent sign at the same spot tell you two different things. Which one must you obey?
options: The temporary sign, because it takes precedence over the other sign
The permanent sign, because it is the fixed, officially installed one
Whichever of the two you saw first
questions.explanation: Most learners assume the bolted-down sign wins. It does not. Where two signs conflict, the temporary one takes precedence, because it is there for a condition that exists on the road today.

questions.prompt: The permanent sign on this road sets the limit at 80, but a temporary sign at the roadworks says 40. What may you drive?
options: 80, because a temporary sign is only a suggestion
40, because the temporary sign overrides the permanent one
80, unless you can actually see workers on the site
questions.explanation: 40. Where a temporary sign conflicts with a permanent one, the temporary sign wins — the bolted-down sign does not outrank it just because it is permanent.

questions.prompt: A temporary Stop sign has been put up while a junction is being rebuilt. What does that sign look like?
options: A yellow octagon reading STOP, because temporary signs are yellow
A yellow triangle with a red border and the word STOP inside it
A red octagon reading STOP, exactly the same shape and colour as any other Stop sign
questions.explanation: "All temporary signs are yellow" is the trap. Control signs — Stop and Yield — keep their normal shape and colour whether they are temporary or permanent, so a temporary Stop is still a red octagon.

questions.prompt: Apart from roadworks, where else will you meet temporary road signs?
options: At accident scenes, where traffic signals are out of order, and controlling traffic at schools and sporting events
Nowhere else, because roadworks are the only lawful use for them
Only on freeways and national roads, where traffic is fastest
questions.explanation: Roadworks are the most common use, not the only one. The manual lists accident scenes, traffic signals out of order, and traffic control at schools and sporting events as non-roadworks uses of temporary signs.

questions.prompt: How long may a temporary road sign stay up?
options: No longer than 24 hours, after which it must be taken down
Anything from a few minutes to several months, for as long as the temporary condition lasts
Up to 14 days, after which it counts as a permanent sign
questions.explanation: There is no fixed lifespan: a temporary sign may be used only for a temporary condition. The manual records temporary regulatory signs standing anywhere from a matter of minutes to periods running into months.

questions.prompt: A temporary warning sign carries the same symbol as the permanent warning sign for that hazard. What is different about it?
options: The border changes from red to yellow and the triangle points downward
Nothing changes, because a temporary warning sign is identical to the permanent one
The background is yellow, while the symbol and the red triangular border stay the same
questions.explanation: The symbol and the red triangle stay the same; the white background turns yellow. Treat that yellow as a prompt to slow down and expect something that is not normally there.

questions.prompt: Which control would you use to stop the vehicle quickly in an emergency?
options: The foot (service) brake
The handbrake
The clutch
questions.explanation: The foot (service) brake is the control for stopping quickly. The handbrake holds a stationary vehicle, and although regulation 149 allows it to double as the emergency brake if the service brake fails, it is not how you make an emergency stop. The clutch disengages the engine from the wheels and does not brake at all.

questions.prompt: Which control keeps the vehicle stationary after you have parked it?
options: The accelerator
The hand (parking) brake
The clutch
questions.explanation: The handbrake/parking brake holds a parked vehicle in place. The accelerator increases speed and the clutch disengages the gearbox — neither holds the vehicle still.

questions.prompt: Which control regulates the fuel supply to the engine to increase the vehicle's speed?
options: The brake
The gear lever
The accelerator
questions.explanation: The accelerator regulates fuel to the engine to increase speed. The brake slows the vehicle and the gear lever selects the ratio — they do not increase speed directly.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the clutch is correct?
options: An automatic vehicle does not have a clutch control
Every vehicle, including automatics, has a clutch control
The clutch is used to stop the vehicle in an emergency
questions.explanation: Automatic vehicles do not have a clutch control. The clutch is used to change gear on a manual, not to perform an emergency stop (that is the foot brake).

questions.prompt: On a manual vehicle, which two controls do you use together to change gear?
options: The accelerator and the brake
The clutch and the gear lever
The handbrake and the steering wheel
questions.explanation: Changing gear on a manual uses the clutch and the gear lever together. The other pairs perform unrelated functions.

questions.prompt: Before changing direction, changing speed or braking, what should a driver always do first?
options: Sound the hooter
Switch on the hazard lights
Check the mirrors
questions.explanation: The manual's standing rule is to check the mirrors first, before any change of speed, direction or braking. The hooter and hazard lights serve different, situational purposes.

questions.prompt: Which control advises other road users of your intention to turn?
options: The direction indicators
The steering wheel
The accelerator
questions.explanation: The direction indicators signal your intention to turn or change direction. The steering wheel changes direction but does not signal it, and the accelerator controls speed.

questions.prompt: Your windscreen has rain on the outside obscuring your view. Which control do you use?
options: The demister
The windscreen wipers
The hazard lights
questions.explanation: The windscreen wipers clear rain and dirt from the outside of the glass. The demister clears misting on the inside, and hazard lights do not affect visibility through the windscreen.

questions.prompt: The inside of your windscreen has misted up on a cold morning. Which control clears it?
options: The windscreen wipers
The horn
The demister
questions.explanation: The demister clears condensation from the inside of the glass. The wipers clear the outside, and the horn is a warning device.

questions.prompt: On a motorcycle, how do you bring the machine to a controlled stop?
options: Use the front brake lever and the rear brake pedal together
Use the front brake lever only
Use the clutch lever only
questions.explanation: A motorcycle is stopped using the front brake lever and rear brake pedal in combination for balanced, controlled braking. Using one brake alone or the clutch is incorrect.

questions.prompt: How should you use the brake during an emergency stop in a vehicle fitted with ABS?
options: Pump the brake pedal rapidly
Apply firm, continuous pressure and keep steering
Use the handbrake instead
questions.explanation: With ABS you apply firm, continuous pressure and hold it — the system prevents wheel lock so you keep steering control. Pumping defeats ABS, and the handbrake is not for emergency stops.

questions.prompt: How should a head restraint (headrest) be positioned?
options: As low as possible for comfort
Removed when not needed
With its top roughly level with the top of your head
questions.explanation: The head restraint should have its top roughly level with the top of your head to limit rearward head movement and reduce whiplash in a rear-end crash. Set too low or removed, it offers little protection.

questions.prompt: When is it appropriate to switch on your hazard lights?
options: When your vehicle is stationary in a hazardous position or broken down
When driving normally in heavy rain
To justify parking in a no-stopping zone
questions.explanation: Hazard lights warn others that your vehicle is stationary in a hazardous position or broken down. They are not for normal driving in rain and do not legitimise illegal stopping.

questions.prompt: You are driving at night on bright (main) beam and a vehicle approaches from the opposite direction. What should you do?
options: Keep bright beam on to see better
Dip to low beam until it has passed
Switch your headlights off
questions.explanation: You must dip to low beam when meeting oncoming traffic so you do not dazzle the other driver, then return to main beam once it has passed. Keeping bright beam on dazzles; switching lights off is dangerous.

questions.prompt: When should you switch on your indicator before turning?
options: While you are turning
Only if another vehicle is close
In good time before you turn
questions.explanation: You should signal in good time before turning so other road users can react. Signalling during the turn is too late, and you must signal regardless of whether another vehicle is near.

questions.prompt: On a motorcycle, when is it most important to have completed your braking?
options: Before entering the turn
While leaned over in the turn
After you have exited the turn
questions.explanation: You should set your speed and complete braking before entering a turn; braking hard (especially the front brake) while leaned over can cause a loss of control. Brakes are best applied upright before the turn.

questions.prompt: Which control disengages the engine from the gearbox so you can change gear?
options: The accelerator
The clutch
The handbrake
questions.explanation: The clutch disconnects the engine from the gearbox to allow a gear change. The accelerator controls speed and the handbrake holds the vehicle still.

questions.prompt: Before and while reversing, which controls help you see what is behind and beside you?
options: The hooter
The demister
The mirrors (and a direct look over your shoulder)
questions.explanation: The rear-view and side mirrors — supported by a direct look around — let you see behind and beside the vehicle before reversing. The hooter and demister do not provide vision.

questions.prompt: Which control actually changes the direction the vehicle travels?
options: The steering wheel
The indicator
The hooter
questions.explanation: The steering wheel changes the vehicle's direction. The indicator only signals your intention to turn, and the hooter is a warning device.

questions.prompt: Which control would you use to warn another road user of danger to avoid a collision?
options: The indicator
The hooter
The wipers
questions.explanation: The hooter (horn) warns other road users of danger to avoid a collision. The indicator signals intention and the wipers clear the windscreen.

questions.prompt: When you press the foot brake, which lights warn the drivers behind you?
options: The headlights
The parking lights
The brake (stop) lights
questions.explanation: Pressing the foot brake lights the brake (stop) lights to warn following drivers you are slowing. Headlights and parking lights are not triggered by braking.

questions.prompt: In a manual vehicle, why do you press the clutch just before coming to a stop?
options: To prevent the engine from stalling
To make the vehicle go faster
To activate the brake lights
questions.explanation: Pressing the clutch just before stopping disconnects the engine so it does not stall. It does not increase speed, and the brake lights are triggered by the brake, not the clutch.

questions.prompt: You are stopped facing uphill and about to pull away. Which control holds the vehicle to prevent rolling back?
options: The accelerator
The handbrake
The demister
questions.explanation: The handbrake holds the vehicle on the hill until you have engine power to pull away, preventing roll-back. The accelerator and demister do not hold the vehicle.

questions.prompt: The rear window has misted up on the inside. Which control clears it?
options: The windscreen wipers
The hooter
The demister
questions.explanation: The demister clears condensation from the inside of the glass, including the rear window. The wipers clear the outside of the windscreen, and the hooter is a warning device.

questions.prompt: When should the driver and passengers fasten their seatbelts?
options: Before the vehicle moves off
Only on the open road
Only if the trip is long
questions.explanation: Fasten before the vehicle moves off. Regulation 213(4) requires an adult occupying a seat that is fitted with a seatbelt to wear it, and the only exception is while reversing or moving in or out of a parking bay. Belts are not optional on short trips and not limited to the open road.

questions.prompt: What is the safety purpose of a correctly set head restraint?
options: To make the seat more comfortable
To reduce whiplash neck injury in a rear-end collision
To support the seatbelt
questions.explanation: A head restraint limits rearward head movement to reduce whiplash in a rear-end crash. Comfort is incidental, and it does not support the seatbelt.

questions.prompt: On a motorcycle, which hand or foot operates the front brake?
options: The left hand (a lever)
The left foot (a pedal)
The right hand (a lever)
questions.explanation: The motorcycle front brake is operated by the right-hand lever. Stopping uses front and rear brakes together.

questions.prompt: Which motorcycle control increases engine speed?
options: The twist-grip throttle (right hand)
The clutch lever (left hand)
The front brake lever
questions.explanation: The right-hand twist-grip throttle increases engine speed on a motorcycle (the equivalent of a car's accelerator). The clutch lever and front brake do not increase speed.

questions.prompt: On a motorcycle, where are the clutch and the gear lever?
options: Clutch = right-hand lever; gear lever = right foot
Clutch = left-hand lever; gear lever = left foot
Both are hand-operated on the right
questions.explanation: On a motorcycle the clutch is the left-hand lever and the gear lever is operated by the left foot. The right side carries the throttle and front brake.

questions.prompt: During hard emergency braking, what does ABS allow the driver to keep?
options: A shorter stopping distance on every surface
The need to pump the pedal
The ability to steer while braking
questions.explanation: ABS prevents wheel lock so you can keep steering while braking hard. It does not guarantee a shorter distance on every surface (it can lengthen it on gravel), and you should not pump the pedal.

questions.prompt: It starts to rain and your view through the windscreen is blurred. Which control do you use?
options: The windscreen wipers
The hazard lights
The hooter
questions.explanation: The windscreen wipers clear rain from the outside of the windscreen to restore your view. Hazard lights and the hooter do not improve forward visibility.

questions.prompt: How does changing gear in an automatic vehicle differ from a manual?
options: An automatic still needs a clutch pedal for each gear change
An automatic has no clutch pedal and selects gears itself
An automatic has no gears at all
questions.explanation: An automatic has no clutch pedal and selects its own gears; the driver only moves the selector (P/R/N/D). There is no clutch for the driver to operate, and the vehicle does have gears.
